They also may not hold a position that leads to conflicts of interest — e.g. the IT manager cannot simultaneously be the DPO, because they would have to supervise their own work.

maturity.level0: Independence not ensured; the DPO holds a position with an obvious conflict of interest (e.g. IT manager, management board)
maturity.level1: DPO holds no obviously conflicting position, but there is no documented assessment of potential conflicts of interest
maturity.level2: Conflicts of interest assessed and ruled out; DPO reports to management, but dismissal protection is not formalised
maturity.level3: Documented conflict-of-interest assessment; DPO reports directly to the highest management level; dismissal protection and non-penalisation contractually anchored

dsbQ5.title: Is the independence of your data protection officer ensured pursuant to Art. 38(3) GDPR (no conflict of interest, no penalisation)?
dsbQ5.tooltip: Art. 38(3) GDPR protects the DPO: they may not be dismissed or penalised for performing their tasks. They report directly to the highest management level. No conflicts of interest may exist (Art. 38(6) GDPR). Typical conflicts: the DPO simultaneously acting as IT manager, managing director, HR manager or marketing manager. Section 38(2) BDSG specifies the dismissal protection.

dsfaQ1.help: A DPIA is a structured assessment of whether a planned data processing operation is particularly risky for the persons affected. Example: you want to introduce video surveillance in the office or use a new CRM system with extensive customer profiles. You must then assess in advance what risks this poses to data subjects and how to minimise them. Without a DPIA you risk fines and potentially unlawful processing.

maturity.level0: No awareness of the DPIA obligation; new processing operations are introduced without any risk assessment
maturity.level1: Awareness of the DPIA obligation exists, but no systematic execution; case-by-case checks only for obviously critical projects
maturity.level2: DPIA is carried out for recognisably high-risk processing, but without a standardised procedure or uniform template
maturity.level3: Standardised DPIA process with templates, threshold analysis and DPO involvement before every high-risk processing operation

dsfaQ1.title: Do you carry out a systematic data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before deploying new processing operations with a high risk to data subjects?
dsfaQ1.tooltip: Art. 35(1) GDPR obliges the controller to carry out a data protection impact assessment before introducing processing operations likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. This applies in particular to the use of new technologies.

dsfaQ2.help: The supervisory authorities have published lists of processing operations that always require a DPIA — e.g. scoring, video surveillance of public areas or large-scale processing of health data. Check the list of your state authority and compare whether your processing operations are on it. If so, you must carry out a DPIA — regardless of your own risk assessment.

maturity.level0: The supervisory authority's blacklist is unknown; no comparison with own processing activities has taken place
maturity.level1: The blacklist is known, but a systematic comparison with own processing activities has not taken place
maturity.level2: The main processing activities were checked against the blacklist, but not completely or without documentation
maturity.level3: Complete, documented comparison of all processing activities with the current blacklist; results are updated when changes occur

dsfaQ2.title: Have you checked which of your processing activities are subject to a mandatory DPIA under the blacklist of the competent supervisory authority?
dsfaQ2.tooltip: Art. 35(3) GDPR lists standard cases of processing requiring a DPIA (profiling, large-scale processing of special categories, systematic monitoring). In addition, supervisory authorities publish mandatory lists (blacklists) pursuant to Art. 35(4) GDPR. In Germany, the list of the DSK (Conference of Data Protection Authorities) is authoritative.

dsfaQ3.help: A DPIA is more than 'we thought about it.' It must contain four things: 1) What exactly is processed, how and why? 2) Is the processing really necessary, or could it be done with less data? 3) What specific risks exist for data subjects (e.g. identity theft, discrimination)? 4) What specific protective measures do you deploy against them? Only when all four points are documented does the DPIA meet the legal requirements.

maturity.level0: No structured DPIA documentation available
maturity.level1: DPIA documentation exists, but essential minimum content is missing (e.g. no risk assessment or no measures)
maturity.level2: DPIA contains all four minimum components, but with varying depth and quality
maturity.level3: Complete DPIA with all minimum content under Art. 35(7) GDPR, including a comprehensible risk assessment and concrete mitigation measures

dsfaQ3.title: Does your DPIA contain the minimum content required by Art. 35(7) GDPR (description, assessment of necessity, risk assessment and mitigation measures)?
dsfaQ3.tooltip: Art. 35(7) GDPR prescribes four minimum components of a DPIA: (a) a systematic description of the processing operations and purposes, (b) an assessment of necessity and proportionality, (c) an assessment of the risks to data subjects, (d) the measures envisaged to address the risks. Without these elements the DPIA is incomplete.

dsfaQ4.help: If your DPIA shows that a high risk to data subjects remains despite all planned safeguards, you may not simply start the processing. You must first consult the competent data protection authority. It will examine your case and may issue recommendations or conditions. Do you have a process for who in your company would trigger this consultation and how it works?

maturity.level0: No awareness of the consultation obligation in case of a high residual risk
maturity.level1: The consultation obligation is known, but no defined process exists for triggering it
maturity.level2: Basic process defined, but thresholds for 'high residual risk' are unclear or undocumented
maturity.level3: Documented escalation process with clear criteria for when the supervisory authority is consulted, including responsibilities and deadlines

dsfaQ4.title: Do you have a procedure for prior consultation of the supervisory authority when a DPIA indicates a high residual risk?
dsfaQ4.tooltip: Art. 36(1) GDPR obliges the controller to consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where the DPIA indicates that the processing would result in a high risk despite the planned safeguards. The authority then has up to 8 weeks to provide written advice (Art. 36(2) GDPR).

dsfaQ5.help: A DPIA is not a one-off document to file away and forget. When something changes — e.g. you add an AI feature, use a new cloud provider or the threat landscape shifts — you must review the DPIA again and update it if necessary. Schedule regular reviews, e.g. annually or upon significant changes.

maturity.level0: Existing DPIAs are never touched again after creation
maturity.level1: Event-driven review in case of obvious changes, but no fixed cycle
maturity.level2: Regular review planned, but not carried out consistently
maturity.level3: Documented review cycle for all DPIAs (at least annually) with trigger criteria for event-driven reassessment

dsfaQ5.title: Do you review existing DPIAs regularly, especially when the risk of the processing changes?
dsfaQ5.tooltip: Art. 35(11) GDPR requires the controller to review a DPIA already carried out when there is a change in the risk represented by the processing. This applies, for example, when new technologies are introduced, the purpose of processing changes or new threat scenarios emerge.

dtQ1.help: Third-country transfer means: data leaves the EEA (EU plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway). This happens more often than you think — e.g. when you use US cloud services (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, AWS), US tools (Mailchimp, Salesforce, Zoom) or engage service providers in India or Ukraine. Create a list of all services and check where the data is actually processed.

maturity.level0: No overview of third-country transfers; it has not been checked whether data leaves the EEA
maturity.level1: Individual obvious third-country transfers are known (e.g. US cloud), but no systematic survey
maturity.level2: Overview of the main third-country transfers available, but incomplete or not updated regularly
maturity.level3: Complete, current overview of all third-country transfers stating the recipient country, the data transferred and the legal basis for each transfer

dtQ1.title: Do you have an overview of whether and to which third countries you transfer personal data?
dtQ1.tooltip: Art. 44 GDPR stipulates that any transfer of personal data to a third country is permitted only if the conditions of Art. 44-49 GDPR are met. Third countries are all countries outside the EEA (EU plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway).

dtQ2.help: If you transfer data to a country without an adequacy decision (e.g. India, Brazil, or the USA without a Privacy Framework certification), you need Standard Contractual Clauses. These are contract texts prescribed by the EU that you conclude with the data recipient. Since the end of 2022 you must use the EU's new SCCs. Old clauses are no longer valid.

maturity.level0: No appropriate safeguards for third-country transfers; data is transferred without a legal basis
maturity.level1: Awareness of the necessity exists; individual SCCs concluded, but not across the board and partly outdated
maturity.level2: Current SCCs (post 2021/914) concluded with the main recipients; individual gaps with smaller service providers
maturity.level3: Current SCCs concluded with all third-country recipients; Transfer Impact Assessments carried out; additional technical measures implemented where necessary

dtQ2.title: Do you use appropriate safeguards for third-country transfers, in particular EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC)?
dtQ2.tooltip: Art. 46(2)(c) GDPR permits third-country transfers on the basis of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC) adopted by the EU Commission. Since 27.12.2022, only the Commission’s new SCCs (Implementing Decision 2021/914) may be used. Additional measures may be required following the CJEU’s Schrems II judgment.

dtQ3.help: An adequacy decision is the simplest solution for third-country transfers: the EU Commission has determined that the recipient country has an adequate level of data protection. Then you need no additional safeguards. For the USA, the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework has applied since July 2023 — but only for certified US companies. Always check whether a decision exists before laboriously concluding SCCs.

maturity.level0: No check for adequacy decisions; third-country transfers are carried out without a legal basis
maturity.level1: Occasional checks in obvious cases, but no systematic review of all transfers
maturity.level2: Adequacy decisions are checked for new service providers, but existing transfers have not been assessed retroactively
maturity.level3: Systematic check of all third-country transfers for an adequacy decision; DPF certification verified for US providers; monitoring for changes to or revocation of decisions

dtQ3.title: For third-country transfers, do you check whether an EU Commission adequacy decision exists for the recipient country?
dtQ3.tooltip: Art. 45 GDPR permits data transfers to third countries for which the EU Commission has determined an adequate level of data protection by decision. Current adequacy decisions exist for, among others: Andorra, Argentina, Canada (partially), the Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Israel, the Isle of Man, Japan, Jersey, New Zealand, South Korea, Switzerland, the UK and the USA (EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework since 10.07.2023). These decisions can be revoked.

dtQ4.help: A Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) is a risk assessment you must carry out when transferring data to a country without an adequacy decision while relying on SCCs. You examine: does that country have laws allowing authorities to access the data? Are the SCCs enforceable there? Are the SCCs sufficient on their own, or do you need additional technical measures such as encryption?

maturity.level0: No awareness of the need for TIAs; no assessment of the legal situation in the recipient country
maturity.level1: Awareness exists, but no TIAs carried out
maturity.level2: TIAs carried out for the main transfers, but not for all; supplementary measures not systematically derived
maturity.level3: TIAs carried out and documented for all relevant third-country transfers; supplementary technical and organisational measures implemented; regular updates when the law changes

dtQ4.title: Do you carry out Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) to evaluate the effectiveness of the safeguards in the recipient country?
dtQ4.tooltip: Art. 46(1)-(2) GDPR requires appropriate safeguards for third-country transfers. Following the CJEU’s Schrems II judgment (C-311/18), controllers must assess whether the SCCs can ensure an adequate level of protection in the specific case — taking into account the legal situation in the recipient country (in particular government access powers). EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 describe the procedure in detail.

dtQ5.help: Art. 49 GDPR provides derogations for specific individual cases — e.g. a customer books a hotel in a third country (contract performance), or you must transfer data for litigation abroad. However, these derogations must NOT be misused as a permanent solution for regular data transfers. If you constantly send customer data to a service provider in a third country, you need SCCs or an adequacy decision — Art. 49 is not sufficient for that.

maturity.level0: Art. 49 GDPR is invoked as the legal basis for regular transfers, although this is not permissible
maturity.level1: Awareness exists that Art. 49 GDPR applies only to exceptions; its use is however not documented or reviewed
maturity.level2: Art. 49 GDPR is invoked only in individual cases; documentation of the conditions exists but is not always complete
maturity.level3: Clear policy that Art. 49 GDPR is applied only in narrowly defined exceptional cases; every use is documented with reasons; regular transfers run exclusively via adequacy decisions or SCCs

dtQ5.title: Do you use derogations under Art. 49 GDPR for third-country transfers only in the narrowly defined statutory cases?
dtQ5.tooltip: Art. 49 GDPR permits third-country transfers in exceptional cases without an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, e.g. with explicit consent (para. 1(a)), for contract performance ((b)-(c)), for important reasons of public interest ((d)), for legal claims ((e)) or vital interests ((f)). These derogations are to be interpreted narrowly and are not suitable for regular, large-scale transfers.

dvQ1.help: If personal data is lost, disclosed without authorisation or altered — e.g. through a hacking attack, a lost USB stick or an email accidentally sent to the wrong recipient — you have at most 72 hours to notify the supervisory authority. This requires a clear procedure: who determines that an incident has occurred? Who decides whether it is notifiable? Who submits the notification?

maturity.level0: No notification process for personal data breaches in place
maturity.level1: Awareness of the 72-hour deadline exists, but no defined procedure and no responsibilities
maturity.level2: Basic notification process documented, but not known to all employees or not practised regularly
maturity.level3: Documented notification process with clear responsibilities, escalation paths, templates for notifying the supervisory authority and regular training

dvQ1.title: Do you have a process to notify personal data breaches to the supervisory authority within 72 hours?
dvQ1.tooltip: Art. 33(1) GDPR obliges the controller to notify a personal data breach to the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours — unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk. Where notification is delayed, reasons for the delay must be given.

dvQ2.help: For every personal data breach you must document internally: what happened? How many people are affected? Which data is affected (e.g. names, bank details)? What are the possible consequences? What have you done about it? You need this documentation both for the notification to the authority and as evidence towards the supervisory authority. Use a form or template for this.

maturity.level0: Personal data breaches are not documented
maturity.level1: Incidents are documented only informally or incompletely
maturity.level2: Documentation template exists, but not all mandatory details under Art. 33(3) GDPR are recorded systematically
maturity.level3: Standardised documentation of every breach with all mandatory details, timestamps, measures taken and the outcome of the risk assessment

dvQ2.title: Are personal data breaches documented internally with all the details required by Art. 33(3) GDPR?
dvQ2.tooltip: Art. 33(3) GDPR requires the notification to the supervisory authority to contain at least: (a) the nature of the breach including categories and number of data subjects affected, (b) the name and contact details of the DPO, (c) the likely consequences of the breach, (d) the measures taken and proposed. Art. 33(5) GDPR additionally requires internal documentation of all breaches.

dvQ3.help: If, for example, customer data including bank details is stolen, you must inform the affected persons directly — not just the supervisory authority, but the people themselves. You must state clearly: what happened? Which data is affected? What can those affected do (e.g. change passwords, inform their bank)? Prepare text templates so no valuable time is lost in an emergency.

maturity.level0: No process for notifying data subjects in place
maturity.level1: Awareness of the notification duty exists, but no criteria or templates
maturity.level2: Basic criteria for the risk assessment defined; notification templates partly available
maturity.level3: Documented risk assessment criteria for high risk; ready-made notification templates in plain language; defined communication channels and responsibilities

dvQ3.title: Do you have a process for notifying data subjects of personal data breaches involving a high risk?
dvQ3.tooltip: Art. 34(1) GDPR requires that data subjects be notified without undue delay when a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. The notification must use clear and plain language.

dvQ4.help: Even if a data protection incident poses no significant risk and is therefore not notifiable, you must still document it internally. Example: an employee sends an email with customer data to the wrong recipient, who deletes it immediately. Not notifiable, but subject to documentation. The supervisory authority can request this record to check whether you take your obligations seriously.

maturity.level0: No documentation of personal data breaches
maturity.level1: Only serious or notified breaches are documented; smaller incidents slip through
maturity.level2: Most breaches are recorded, but documentation is not uniform or complete
maturity.level3: Complete record of all personal data breaches with assessment, measures and the reasons for the notification decision; regular analysis for prevention

dvQ4.title: Do you keep a complete record of all personal data breaches — including those that were not notifiable?
dvQ4.tooltip: Art. 33(5) GDPR obliges the controller to document all personal data breaches, including the related facts, effects and remedial measures taken. This documentation must enable the supervisory authority to verify compliance — which means it must also cover incidents not subject to notification.

dvQ5.help: You can avoid the obligation to notify data subjects if you have taken good protective measures in advance. The most important example: encryption. If an encrypted laptop is stolen, the data cannot be read — hence no high risk and no notification obligation. The same applies to pseudonymisation. Invest in preventive measures and spare yourself the reputational damage in an emergency.

maturity.level0: No preventive protective measures such as encryption or pseudonymisation implemented
maturity.level1: Individual measures exist (e.g. disk encryption), but not across the board and not documented
maturity.level2: Key data stores are encrypted; pseudonymisation is used for individual processing operations
maturity.level3: Comprehensive encryption of all mobile devices and data transfers; pseudonymisation wherever possible; documented mapping of protective measures per processing activity

dvQ5.title: Have you implemented technical and organisational measures that can render notification of data subjects unnecessary under Art. 34(3) GDPR?
dvQ5.tooltip: Art. 34(3) GDPR provides that notification of data subjects is not required if: (a) appropriate protective measures such as encryption were applied, (b) subsequent measures have eliminated the high risk, or (c) notification would involve disproportionate effort (in which case a public communication is required).

ewQ1.help: Before processing personal data, you need legal permission to do so. The most common bases are: contract performance (e.g. delivery address for orders), legal obligation (e.g. payroll tax filing) or consent (e.g. newsletter). The legal basis should be documented for every processing operation in your record. If it is missing, the processing is unlawful.

maturity.level0: Legal bases are not identified or documented for any processing operation
maturity.level1: The legal basis is known for individual processing operations, but not systematically documented
maturity.level2: Legal bases are documented for most processing operations; occasionally missing or unclear
maturity.level3: The legal basis for every processing activity is clearly documented, regularly reviewed and updated when changes occur

ewQ1.title: Have you identified and documented a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR for every processing activity?
ewQ1.tooltip: Art. 6(1) GDPR lists six possible legal bases: consent ((a)), contract performance ((b)), legal obligation ((c)), vital interests ((d)), public interest ((e)) and legitimate interest ((f)). Every processing operation requires at least one of these bases. Section 26 BDSG contains special rules for employee data.

ewQ2.help: If you rely on consent as the legal basis — e.g. for newsletters or marketing cookies — you must be able to prove that the person actually consented. This includes: when was consent given? How were they informed? What exactly was permitted? Double opt-in for newsletters is a good example: the person signs up, receives a confirmation email and clicks the link — all of which is logged.

maturity.level0: No evidence of consents given is available
maturity.level1: Consent is obtained, but the evidence is patchy (e.g. no timestamp, no wording stored)
maturity.level2: Consents are documented with timestamp and wording, but not centrally managed or regularly reviewed
maturity.level3: Complete, audit-proof documentation of all consents with timestamp, exact wording, consent channel and central management

ewQ2.title: For processing based on consent, can you demonstrate that the data subject has validly consented?
ewQ2.tooltip: Art. 7(1) GDPR places the burden of proof on the controller: they must be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous (Art. 4(11) GDPR). Section 26(2) BDSG generally requires written form for employee consent.

ewQ3.help: If someone signs up for your newsletter with a click, they must be able to unsubscribe just as easily — e.g. via an unsubscribe link in every email. It is not sufficient if data subjects have to write a letter or call. You must also ensure that no more emails are actually sent after withdrawal. Test this regularly.

maturity.level0: No withdrawal mechanism exists; data subjects have practically no way to withdraw consent
maturity.level1: Withdrawal is possible, but cumbersome (e.g. only by email or letter) and not as easy as giving consent
maturity.level2: Simple withdrawal mechanism in place (e.g. unsubscribe link), but the technical cessation of processing is not always ensured
maturity.level3: Withdrawal is as easy as giving consent; after withdrawal, processing is stopped automatically and verifiably

ewQ3.title: Can data subjects withdraw their consent easily at any time, and is processing actually stopped after withdrawal?
ewQ3.tooltip: Art. 7(3) GDPR guarantees the right to withdraw consent at any time. Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. Before giving consent, the data subject must be informed of the right to withdraw. The lawfulness of processing carried out before withdrawal remains unaffected.

ewQ4.help: If your online service, app or web shop can also be used by people under 16, you need special precautions: you must verify age and, for under-16s, obtain and verify parental consent. This affects e.g. registrations, newsletter sign-ups or in-app purchases. If you run a purely B2B service, this topic is usually not relevant.

maturity.level0: No age verification or special safeguards for minors implemented
maturity.level1: Age query in place, but no verification and no process for parental consent
maturity.level2: Age check and basic process for parental consent in place, but verification is patchy
maturity.level3: Robust age verification with demonstrable collection and verification of parental consent; regular review of the mechanism

ewQ4.title: Have you implemented special safeguards for the consent of minors in relation to information society services?
ewQ4.tooltip: Art. 8 GDPR governs children’s consent for information society services (e.g. online services, apps). In Germany the age limit is 16 years (Art. 8(1) GDPR; Germany has not set a different age limit). For children under 16, consent or authorisation by the holder of parental responsibility is required. The controller must make reasonable efforts to verify this.

ewQ5.help: Special categories of data include e.g. health data (sick notes, occupational reintegration), religious affiliation (church tax), trade union membership or biometric data (fingerprint scanners). This data may only be processed under strict conditions. Where no statutory permission applies, you need explicit consent — particularly clear and prominent, not hidden in terms and conditions.

maturity.level0: No check whether special categories of data are processed; no specific consents obtained
maturity.level1: Awareness of special categories of data exists, but no systematic check or separate consents
maturity.level2: Special categories of data are identified; explicit consent is obtained, but not consistently in all cases
maturity.level3: Complete overview of special categories of data; explicit, separately documented consents with additional safeguards under Section 22 BDSG

ewQ5.title: Do you obtain explicit consent for processing special categories of personal data where no other exception under Art. 9(2) GDPR applies?
ewQ5.tooltip: Art. 9(1) GDPR prohibits in principle the processing of special categories of data (health, religion, ethnic origin, political opinions, trade union membership, genetics, biometrics, sex life). Art. 9(2)(a) GDPR permits processing with explicit consent. Section 22 BDSG contains additional conditions and safeguards.

pbdQ1.help: Privacy by design means: data protection is considered from the very beginning, not bolted on afterwards. For example, when planning a new customer database, consider already in the planning phase: which data do we really need? How long do we keep it? How do we protect it? Who has access? This is more efficient and safer than laboriously retrofitting later.

maturity.level0: Data protection is not considered when introducing new systems or processes
maturity.level1: Data protection is raised for obviously critical projects, but not systematically included in planning
maturity.level2: Checklist or guideline for data protection in new projects available; DPO is involved in larger projects
maturity.level3: Standardised process: every new system, product or procedure undergoes a data protection review in the planning phase with documented sign-off by the DPO

pbdQ1.title: Do you take data protection requirements into account from the planning and development stage of new systems, products and processes (privacy by design)?
pbdQ1.tooltip: Art. 25(1) GDPR requires the controller, both at the time of determining the means for processing and at the time of processing itself, to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data protection principles effectively. The state of the art, implementation costs and risks must be taken into account.

pbdQ2.help: Privacy by default means: the most privacy-friendly setting is the default. Example: when you create an online form, only the mandatory fields are pre-filled — not optional newsletter sign-ups or marketing consents. In a social media profile, visibility is set to 'private' by default. In your CRM, employees only see the data they need for their tasks.

maturity.level0: No privacy-friendly default settings; maximum data collection and accessibility as the default
maturity.level1: Individual systems have restrictive default settings, but there is no consistent principle
maturity.level2: Privacy by default is considered for most new systems; existing systems have been partly adapted
maturity.level3: All systems are configured by default for minimal data processing and minimal accessibility; regular review of the default settings

pbdQ2.title: Do you ensure that your systems process, by default, only the personal data necessary for the specific purpose (privacy by default)?
pbdQ2.tooltip: Art. 25(2) GDPR requires that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose of processing is processed. This applies to the amount collected, the extent of processing, the storage period and accessibility. By default, personal data must not be made accessible to an indefinite number of persons without the data subject’s intervention.

pbdQ3.help: Data minimisation means: collect only what you really need. Do you really need date of birth, gender and phone number for a newsletter — or is the email address enough? Do you really need the customer's company size for a delivery? Review every form field, every database column: is this really necessary, or are we collecting it 'just in case'?

maturity.level0: No necessity check; data is collected 'in reserve' and 'just in case'
maturity.level1: Awareness of data minimisation exists, but no systematic review of the data collected
maturity.level2: Key forms and processes reviewed for necessity; individual data fields removed, but no comprehensive implementation
maturity.level3: Systematic necessity review of all data collection; documented justification for every data field collected; regular review of existing data holdings

pbdQ3.title: Do you apply the principle of data minimisation — collecting and storing only the data actually necessary for the specific purpose?
pbdQ3.tooltip: Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR establishes the principle of data minimisation: personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing. This principle is a core element of privacy by design and affects the design of forms, databases, processes and interfaces.

pbdQ4.help: Certifications such as ISO 27701 (privacy information management system) or industry-specific codes of conduct can help you demonstrate compliance with privacy by design. This is particularly useful towards the supervisory authority, in tenders or towards customers. A certification does not protect against fines, but can serve as evidence of your efforts and reduce the fine risk.

maturity.level0: No certifications or codes of conduct in the data protection area; no evidence of compliance efforts
maturity.level1: Interest in certification exists, but no concrete steps taken
maturity.level2: Individual measures follow recognised standards (e.g. ISO 27001/27701), but no formal certification
maturity.level3: Formal data protection certification (e.g. ISO 27701) or participation in approved codes of conduct; regular re-certification; the certificate is actively used as compliance documentation

pbdQ4.title: Do you use certifications or approved codes of conduct to demonstrate compliance with privacy by design?
pbdQ4.tooltip: Art. 25(3) GDPR provides that approved certification mechanisms pursuant to Art. 42 GDPR may be used as an element to demonstrate compliance with privacy by design and privacy by default requirements. Likewise, approved codes of conduct pursuant to Art. 40 GDPR may be taken into account in the assessment.

pbdQ5.help: Data you no longer need must be deleted — not only when someone asks, but automatically once the defined retention period expires. Example: automatically delete applicant data 6 months after rejection, cookie data after the defined period, inactive customer accounts after 3 years. Manual deletion is error-prone — build in automatic mechanisms.

maturity.level0: No defined retention periods; data is kept indefinitely; no deletion mechanisms
maturity.level1: Retention periods are partly defined, but deletion happens only manually and irregularly
maturity.level2: Retention periods defined for the main data categories; individual automated deletion mechanisms exist, but not across the board
maturity.level3: Deletion concept for all data categories with defined periods; automated deletion mechanisms in all relevant systems; regular review of implementation and logging

pbdQ5.title: Have you implemented automated deletion mechanisms that automatically erase personal data once the processing purpose or retention period has expired?
pbdQ5.tooltip: Art. 5(1)(e) GDPR establishes the principle of storage limitation: personal data may be stored only for as long as necessary for the purposes. Privacy by design requires that deletion mechanisms be built into the system architecture from the outset, not retrofitted.

tomQ1.help: Encryption means: data is transformed so that only authorised persons can read it. This covers e.g. email encryption, HTTPS on your website, encrypted hard drives and encrypted database connections. Pseudonymisation means: the direct personal reference is removed and replaced by a code. Both measures considerably reduce the risk in the event of data breaches.

maturity.level0: Neither encryption nor pseudonymisation in use; personal data is stored and transmitted in plain text
maturity.level1: Basic encryption in place (e.g. HTTPS on the website), but no encryption of storage media or databases; no pseudonymisation
maturity.level2: Encryption for data transfers and mobile devices; pseudonymisation for individual processing operations (e.g. analytics)
maturity.level3: End-to-end encryption at rest and in transit; pseudonymisation wherever possible; regular review of the mechanisms used against the state of the art

tomQ1.title: Do you use encryption and pseudonymisation as technical measures to protect personal data?
tomQ1.tooltip: Art. 32(1)(a) GDPR explicitly names pseudonymisation and encryption as appropriate technical measures to ensure a level of protection appropriate to the risk.

tomQ2.help: You must ensure three protection goals: confidentiality (only those authorised see the data — e.g. through an authorisation concept and passwords), integrity (data is not altered without authorisation — e.g. through checksums and change logs), availability (systems work when needed — e.g. through backups and redundant systems). Document which specific measures you have implemented for each protection goal.

maturity.level0: No systematic measures for confidentiality, integrity or availability
maturity.level1: Basic measures in place (e.g. password protection, antivirus software), but no comprehensive authorisation concept and no availability safeguards
maturity.level2: Authorisation concept implemented; backups in place; integrity checks for important systems, but not across the board
maturity.level3: Documented authorisation concept following the need-to-know principle; automated integrity checks; highly available systems with tested recovery procedures

tomQ2.title: Do you ensure the confidentiality, integrity and availability of your systems and services that process personal data?
tomQ2.tooltip: Art. 32(1)(b) GDPR requires the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems and services. Confidentiality: only authorised persons have access. Integrity: data is not altered without authorisation. Availability: systems function when needed.

tomQ3.help: If your systems fail due to a ransomware attack, server damage, fire or water damage — how quickly can you restore the personal data? 'Rapidly' means: within hours, not weeks. This requires tested backups stored separately from the main system and a documented recovery plan. Test regularly whether recovery actually works.

maturity.level0: No backup or recovery strategy in place
maturity.level1: Backups are created but not tested; recovery time and procedure are unclear
maturity.level2: Regular backups with occasional recovery tests; recovery time is around 24-48 hours
maturity.level3: Automated backups with regularly tested recovery within defined time targets; separate storage; documented contingency plan

tomQ3.title: Can you rapidly restore the availability of personal data after a physical or technical incident?
tomQ3.tooltip: Art. 32(1)(c) GDPR requires the ability to restore the availability of and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident. Art. 32(1)(d) GDPR additionally requires a process for regularly testing and evaluating the effectiveness of the measures.

tomQ4.help: It is not enough to introduce protective measures once and never check them again. You must regularly test whether your measures are still effective. This can be an annual review by your DPO or an external provider, a penetration test of your systems or the evaluation of security incidents. Document the results and derive improvement measures.

maturity.level0: No review of the effectiveness of protective measures
maturity.level1: Occasional, event-driven reviews (e.g. after an incident), but no regular cycle
maturity.level2: Annual review of the main measures; results are documented, but improvements are not implemented systematically
maturity.level3: Regular audit cycle with internal and external reviews; penetration tests; documented results with a binding action plan and follow-up

tomQ4.title: Do you have a procedure for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of your technical and organisational measures?
tomQ4.tooltip: Art. 32(1)(d) GDPR explicitly requires a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures. This includes internal audits, penetration tests, vulnerability analyses and the evaluation of security incidents.

tomQ5.help: The GDPR does not expect measures at any price, but proportionate measures. A small craft business that only stores customer addresses needs different measures than a hospital with patient data. When selecting, consider: what is technically feasible today (state of the art)? What does implementation cost? How sensitive is the data? How likely and severe would a data loss be? Document this weighing.

maturity.level0: No documented weighing when selecting protective measures; measures are random or have grown historically
maturity.level1: Protective measures are selected based on availability and cost, but without a systematic risk assessment
maturity.level2: Risk-based selection of protective measures for the main processing operations; the state of the art is considered but not updated regularly
maturity.level3: Documented, risk-based selection of all protective measures considering the state of the art, costs, processing purpose and risk assessment; annual update

tomQ5.title: When selecting your protective measures, do you take into account the state of the art, implementation costs and the nature, scope and purposes of the processing?
tomQ5.tooltip: Art. 32(1) GDPR requires that the selection of protective measures take into account the state of the art, implementation costs, the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the likelihood and severity of the risk. Art. 32(2) GDPR requires the assessment to consider in particular risks from destruction, loss, alteration or unauthorised access.

vvQ1.help: The record of processing activities is your company's central data protection document. It lists every activity in which personal data is processed — e.g. payroll, customer database, newsletter dispatch, applicant management. Certain details must be documented for each activity. The supervisory authority can request this record at any time.

maturity.level0: No record of processing activities exists
maturity.level1: Individual processing activities are known, but not systematically documented
maturity.level2: A record of processing activities exists, but does not contain all mandatory details or all processing operations
maturity.level3: Complete record of processing activities with all mandatory details under Art. 30(1) GDPR for every processing activity

vvQ1.title: Do you maintain a complete record of all processing activities with the mandatory details required by Art. 30(1) GDPR?
vvQ1.tooltip: Art. 30(1) GDPR obliges every controller to maintain a record of all processing activities. Mandatory entries include: name and contact details of the controller, purposes of processing, categories of data subjects and personal data, categories of recipients, transfers to third countries, erasure deadlines and technical and organisational measures.

vvQ2.help: For every processing operation in your record you must state: WHY do you process the data (e.g. contract performance, legal obligation)? WHOSE data is affected (customers, employees, suppliers)? WHICH data exactly (name, address, bank details, health data)? These entries must be up to date — if you launch a new online shop, for example, it must be added promptly.

maturity.level0: Purposes, categories of data subjects and data categories are not documented
maturity.level1: Rough entries exist, but they are incomplete or outdated
maturity.level2: Mostly documented correctly, but updates after changes are not made promptly
maturity.level3: All processing operations with current, correct entries on purposes, categories of data subjects and data categories; a change process is established

vvQ2.title: Are the purposes of processing, the categories of data subjects and the data categories documented correctly and kept up to date in your record of processing activities?
vvQ2.tooltip: Art. 30(1)(b)-(d) GDPR requires documentation of the purposes of processing, the categories of data subjects (e.g. customers, employees, applicants) and the categories of personal data (e.g. contact details, bank details, health data). These entries must reflect the actual processing operations.

vvQ3.help: For every data processing operation you must define when the data will be deleted — e.g. applicant data 6 months after rejection, invoice data after 10 years (statutory retention obligation). In addition, you describe how the data is protected — e.g. encryption, access restriction, pseudonymisation. These entries belong in your record of processing activities.

maturity.level0: Neither erasure deadlines nor protective measures are documented in the record
maturity.level1: Blanket reference to 'statutory periods'; no specific deadlines per processing operation; protective measures missing or only generic
maturity.level2: Erasure deadlines defined for most processing operations; protective measures described in general terms but not per processing operation
maturity.level3: Specific erasure deadlines for each data category with legal basis; protective measures documented per processing operation and reviewed regularly

vvQ3.title: Have you documented the envisaged erasure deadlines and a general description of the technical and organisational protective measures in your record of processing activities?
vvQ3.tooltip: Art. 30(1)(f)-(g) GDPR requires stating the envisaged time limits for erasure of the different categories of data and a general description of the technical and organisational security measures pursuant to Art. 32(1) GDPR. ‘Where possible’ is not an exemption here but the supervisory authorities’ expectation.

vvQ4.help: If your company processes data for other companies — e.g. as an IT service provider, payroll office, hosting provider or marketing agency — you are a processor and must keep your own record. It lists which data you process for which clients. Even if you are mainly a controller, there may be areas in which you act as a processor.

maturity.level0: No check performed on whether the company also acts as a processor; no corresponding record exists
maturity.level1: Awareness exists that acting as a processor requires its own record, but this has not been implemented
maturity.level2: Record under Art. 30(2) GDPR exists, but is incomplete or not up to date
maturity.level3: Complete, current processor record with all mandatory details, clearly separated from the controller's record of processing activities

vvQ4.title: Do you also maintain your own record of processing activities as a processor pursuant to Art. 30(2) GDPR?
vvQ4.tooltip: Art. 30(2) GDPR also obliges the processor to maintain a record. It contains: name and contact details of the processor and of each controller, categories of processing, transfers to third countries where applicable, and a general description of the protective measures. This is a separate record, independent of the controller’s record of processing activities.

vvQ5.help: The supervisory authority can request your record of processing activities at any time — e.g. during an audit or after a complaint. You must then be able to present it promptly. This means: it must be up to date, not compiled only upon request. The exemption for small companies under 250 employees almost never applies in practice, because almost every company processes personal data regularly.

maturity.level0: No presentable record exists
maturity.level1: A record exists, but it is outdated or incomplete and cannot be presented at short notice
maturity.level2: The record is presentable, but is updated only when prompted and not maintained regularly
maturity.level3: The record is reviewed and updated at least quarterly; the supervisory authority can receive a current version at any time

vvQ5.title: Can your record of processing activities be presented to the supervisory authority on request at any time, and is it updated regularly?
vvQ5.tooltip: Art. 30(4) GDPR requires that the record be made available to the supervisory authority on request. Art. 30(5) GDPR contains an exemption for organisations with fewer than 250 employees, which however only applies if the processing is not regular, does not involve special categories of data and poses no risk — in practice this exemption rarely applies.

q1.description: Art. 35 GDPR requires a DPIA for processing with a high risk to the rights of data subjects, e.g. profiling, video surveillance or processing of special categories of data.
q1.title: Do you carry out a data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing?

q10.description: Art. 28 GDPR requires written data processing agreements with instruction-boundness, TOMs, sub-processor approval and support with data subject rights.
q10.title: Have you concluded GDPR-compliant contracts with all processors?

q2.description: Art. 30 GDPR requires documentation of all processing operations with purpose, legal basis, recipients, erasure deadlines and technical and organisational measures.
q2.title: Do you maintain a complete record of all processing activities?

q3.description: Art. 6-7 GDPR require freely given, informed and unambiguous consent with documented evidence and a simple withdrawal option.
q3.title: Is consent obtained verifiably and can it be withdrawn at any time?

q4.description: Art. 15-21 GDPR guarantee data subject rights (access, erasure, rectification, data portability, objection) with a response deadline of one month.
q4.title: Can you handle access, erasure and rectification requests within one month?

q5.description: Art. 33-34 GDPR require notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours and, where applicable, notification of data subjects in case of high risk.
q5.title: Is there a process for reporting personal data breaches within 72 hours?

q6.description: Art. 37-39 GDPR, Section 38 BDSG: from 20 employees engaged in data processing, or where the core business involves large-scale processing, a DPO is mandatory.
q6.title: Has a data protection officer been designated and involved in all relevant processes?

q7.description: Art. 44-49 GDPR require an adequacy decision, Standard Contractual Clauses or binding corporate rules for third-country transfers (e.g. USA, India).
q7.title: Are transfers of personal data to third countries secured by appropriate safeguards?

q8.description: Art. 32 GDPR requires measures appropriate to the risk, such as encryption, pseudonymisation, access controls and regular effectiveness reviews.
q8.title: Are technical and organisational measures in place to protect personal data?

q9.description: Art. 25 GDPR (privacy by design/default): data protection must be built into technical systems from the outset, with privacy-friendly default settings.
q9.title: Is data protection considered from the outset when developing new systems and processes?

av1.description: Review all existing contracts with processors for completeness under Art. 28(1) and (3) GDPR. The contract must govern the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, data types, erasure obligations and TOMs.
av1.firstStep: Create a list of all external service providers with data access and check whether DPAs exist and are up to date.
av1.title: Review data processing agreements under Art. 28 GDPR

av2.description: Before engagement, check whether the processor provides sufficient guarantees for data protection and data security (Art. 28(1) GDPR). This includes certifications, security concepts and audit reports.
av2.firstStep: Request current ISO 27001 certificates, SOC 2 reports or comparable evidence from all cloud and SaaS providers.
av2.title: Carry out due diligence on processors

av3.checklist:
Review and update data processing agreements per Art. 28 GDPR
Document and approve sub-processors
Verify technical and organizational measures of processors
av3.description: Ensure that processors do not engage sub-processors without your approval (Art. 28(2) and (4) GDPR). You must be informed about sub-processors and have a right to object.
av3.firstStep: Request a current list of sub-processors from all main service providers and have changes reported to you.
av3.title: Establish sub-processor management

br1.description: Create a systematic process for handling access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection and data portability requests under Art. 15-22 GDPR. The process must govern responsibilities, deadlines and documentation.
br1.firstStep: Designate a central point of contact for data subject requests and define the workflow from receipt to response.
br1.title: Establish a process for data subject requests

br2.description: Ensure that all data subject requests are answered within one month, as prescribed by Art. 12(3) GDPR. For complex requests the deadline can be extended by two months, but this must be justified.
br2.firstStep: Set up a ticket system or email inbox with automatic deadline monitoring for data subject requests.
br2.title: Meet the one-month deadline for data subject requests

br3.description: Develop technical solutions for efficiently implementing the right to erasure (Art. 17 GDPR) and data portability (Art. 20 GDPR). This reduces manual effort and minimises sources of error during processing.
br3.firstStep: Check your systems for functions for automated data extraction and deletion (e.g. via API or admin interface).
br3.title: Implement automated erasure and data portability

dsb1.description: Check whether your company is obliged to designate a data protection officer (Art. 37 GDPR, Section 38 BDSG). This applies in particular to core activities involving systematic monitoring, large-scale processing of sensitive data or from 20 persons with data access.
dsb1.firstStep: Count how many employees are permanently engaged in processing personal data (from 20: designation obligation under Section 38 BDSG).
dsb1.title: Check the obligation to designate a data protection officer

dsb2.description: Ensure that your data protection officer can act free of instructions, has the necessary resources and is involved early in all data protection matters, as required by Art. 38 GDPR.
dsb2.firstStep: Provide the DPO with a budget for training, tools and legal advice and formalise their involvement in project kick-offs.
dsb2.title: Ensure the DPO's independence and resources

dsb3.description: Define the specific tasks of the data protection officer under Art. 39 GDPR: informing, advising, monitoring compliance, cooperating with the supervisory authority and acting as contact for data subjects. Clarify reporting lines to management.
dsb3.firstStep: Create a written role description for the DPO with tasks, powers and reporting lines.
dsb3.title: Define the DPO's tasks and reporting lines

dsfa1.description: Carry out a data protection impact assessment for all processing operations with a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Under Art. 35(1) and (3) GDPR, this is mandatory for large-scale processing of sensitive data or systematic profiling.
dsfa1.firstStep: Create a list of all current processing operations and assess them against the DPIA criteria under Art. 35(3) GDPR.
dsfa1.title: Carry out a DPIA for high-risk processing

dsfa2.description: Compare your processing activities against the blacklist and whitelist of your competent supervisory authority. Under Art. 35(4) GDPR, these lists specify when a DPIA is mandatory or not necessary.
dsfa2.firstStep: Open the DPIA list of your state data protection authority (e.g. the DSK blacklist) and compare your processing operations.
dsfa2.title: Check the supervisory authority's DPIA blacklist and whitelist

dsfa3.checklist:
Identify high-risk processing activities
Conduct data protection impact assessment per Art. 35 GDPR
Document and implement risk mitigation measures
dsfa3.description: Implement a standardised methodology for carrying out data protection impact assessments under Art. 35(7) GDPR. The methodology should cover risk assessment, mitigation measures and, where necessary, consultation of the supervisory authority under Art. 36 GDPR.
dsfa3.firstStep: Define a DPIA template with the mandatory content under Art. 35(7) GDPR (description, necessity, risk assessment, mitigation measures).
dsfa3.title: Establish a systematic DPIA methodology

dt1.description: Record all transfers of personal data to countries outside the EU/EEA under Chapter V GDPR (Art. 44-49). This includes cloud services, international group structures, support providers and web tracking tools.
dt1.firstStep: Check all processors and cloud services for server locations outside the EU/EEA (e.g. USA, Switzerland, UK post-Brexit).
dt1.title: Identify and document all third-country transfers

dt2.description: Secure third-country transfers with appropriate safeguards: an EU Commission adequacy decision or Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) under Art. 46(2)(c) GDPR. Since Schrems II, an additional case-by-case assessment is required.
dt2.firstStep: Conclude the current EU Standard Contractual Clauses (2021) with all third-country providers or check for adequacy decisions.
dt2.title: Implement Standard Contractual Clauses or adequacy decisions

dt3.checklist:
Identify and document third-country transfers
Review adequacy decisions and standard contractual clauses
Conduct Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA)
dt3.description: Carry out a Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) for every third-country transfer under Art. 46(2) GDPR. It assesses whether the level of data protection in the destination country can be raised to the EU level through additional measures (e.g. encryption).
dt3.firstStep: Select your most critical third-country transfers and use the EDPB recommendations to assess whether government access is possible in the destination country.
dt3.title: Carry out a Transfer Impact Assessment

dv1.description: Implement a process that enables personal data breaches to be notified to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of them, as required by Art. 33(1) GDPR. Late notifications can result in fines.
dv1.firstStep: Create a notification template with all mandatory details under Art. 33(3) GDPR and store the contact details of your supervisory authority.
dv1.title: Set up a 72-hour breach notification process

dv2.description: Keep a record of all personal data breaches under Art. 33(5) GDPR. Incidents that are not notifiable must also be documented in order to fulfil the accountability obligation and identify patterns.
dv2.firstStep: Set up a table or database logging the type of breach, affected data categories, time, remedial measures and notification status.
dv2.title: Create documentation of all personal data breaches

dv3.checklist:
Establish data breach process per Art. 33/34 GDPR
Integrate reporting deadlines (72h) into incident response plan
Train employees on data protection incidents
dv3.description: Create a complete contingency plan for personal data breaches covering detection, assessment, containment, notification of the supervisory authority and data subjects (Art. 33-34 GDPR) and lessons learned.
dv3.firstStep: Run a tabletop exercise with a simulated data protection incident to identify gaps in the current process.
dv3.title: Develop a comprehensive breach response plan

ew1.description: Check for every processing operation whether a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR exists. Consents must meet the requirements of Art. 7 GDPR (freely given, informed, unambiguous, demonstrable).
ew1.firstStep: Create a list of all data processing operations and enter the respective legal basis (contract, consent, legitimate interest etc.).
ew1.title: Review the legal bases of all processing activities

ew2.description: Ensure that data subjects can withdraw their consent at any time as easily as it was given (Art. 7(3) GDPR). This applies to newsletters, cookies, marketing purposes and all other consent-based processing.
ew2.firstStep: Check all systems processing consent (newsletter tool, cookie banner) for working withdrawal options.
ew2.title: Enable easy withdrawal of consent

ew3.checklist:
Review consent texts for voluntariness and specificity
Implement technical withdrawal mechanisms
Introduce consent management system
ew3.description: Implement a central system for managing all consents that fulfils the evidence obligations under Art. 7(1) and the accountability obligation under Art. 5(2) GDPR. The system should log the time of consent, its scope, withdrawal and evidence.
ew3.firstStep: Evaluate consent management platforms (e.g. OneTrust, Usercentrics) or develop an internal tracking system for consents.
ew3.title: Introduce a central consent management system

pbd1.description: Ensure that data protection is considered from the design and development phase of IT systems (Art. 25(1) GDPR). Privacy by design means: data protection as the standard, not as an afterthought.
pbd1.firstStep: Add a mandatory 'data protection requirements' review item to your project checklists before implementation.
pbd1.title: Integrate data protection requirements into development processes

pbd2.description: Configure all systems by default so that only the data necessary for the specific processing purpose is processed (Art. 25(2) GDPR). Users must not be nudged into disclosing unnecessary data through pre-ticked boxes.
pbd2.firstStep: Check all forms and registration screens: are optional fields really optional and not pre-filled?
pbd2.title: Implement privacy-friendly default settings

pbd3.description: Anchor privacy by design systematically in your development processes under Art. 25 GDPR. This can be done through privacy impact assessments, data protection checklists in agile sprints or privacy champions in teams.
pbd3.firstStep: Train all developers and product owners in the basic principles of privacy by design (data minimisation, transparency, control).
pbd3.title: Implement a privacy-by-design framework

tom1.description: Record and document all technical and organisational measures for protecting personal data under Art. 32(1) GDPR. This includes access control, encryption, pseudonymisation, availability and regular testing.
tom1.firstStep: Create a TOM register with categories such as physical access control, data backup and encryption, and assign concrete measures to each category.
tom1.title: Document technical and organisational measures

tom2.description: Implement encryption and pseudonymisation as central protective measures under Art. 32(1)(a) GDPR. This reduces the risk in the event of data breaches and can eliminate notification obligations.
tom2.firstStep: Enable encryption on all mobile devices (BitLocker, FileVault) and check TLS for all data transfers.
tom2.title: Deploy encryption and pseudonymisation

tom3.checklist:
Inventory all technical and organizational measures
Assess measures for adequacy per Art. 32 GDPR
Establish regular effectiveness reviews
tom3.description: Carry out regular tests and reviews of your technical and organisational measures, as required by Art. 32(1)(d) GDPR. This includes penetration tests, backup restores and access logs.
tom3.firstStep: Schedule an annual audit at which all TOMs are checked for currency and effectiveness.
tom3.title: Establish regular effectiveness reviews of the TOMs

vv1.description: Create a complete record of all processing activities under Art. 30(1) GDPR. This record is required evidence for the accountability obligation under Art. 5(2) GDPR and the basis of every data protection audit.
vv1.firstStep: Record all systems and applications in which personal data is processed (HR system, CRM, email, web shop etc.).
vv1.title: Create a record of processing activities under Art. 30 GDPR

vv2.checklist:
Record all processing activities
Create records of processing per Art. 30 GDPR
Document responsibilities and legal bases
vv2.description: Ensure that your record of processing activities contains all mandatory details under Art. 30(1)(a)-(g) GDPR: name of the controller, purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, third-country transfers, erasure deadlines and technical/organisational measures.
vv2.firstStep: Check your existing record of processing activities against the checklist in Art. 30(1) GDPR and identify missing entries.
vv2.title: Document all mandatory details in the record of processing activities

vv3.description: Establish a process for regularly reviewing and updating the record of processing activities under Art. 30(4) GDPR. New processing operations, changed purposes or decommissioned systems must be recorded promptly.
vv3.firstStep: Set a quarterly reminder for all departments to report changes to processing activities.
vv3.title: Regularly update and review the record of processing activities

kritis.name: KRITIS
kritis.description: Protection of critical infrastructures under the BSI Act
kritis.title: KRITIS Additional Requirements
kritis.subtitle: Extended obligations for critical infrastructure operators under §§31, 39 BSIG
kritis.intro: Critical infrastructure operators are subject to additional obligations beyond standard NIS2 requirements, particularly regarding attack detection and evidence management.

attackDetection.title: Attack Detection Systems (§31 BSIG)
attackDetection.description: KRITIS operators must deploy attack detection systems that meet the state of the art.

continuousMonitoring.title: Continuous Monitoring
continuousMonitoring.description: Systems must continuously identify and evaluate threats and initiate appropriate measures.

evidence.title: Evidence Obligation (§39 BSIG)
evidence.description: KRITIS operators must regularly demonstrate compliance with requirements to the BSI.

audits.title: BSI Audits
audits.description: The BSI may verify compliance through on-site inspections or by requesting evidence.

higherPenalties.title: Higher Penalties
higherPenalties.description: Violations of KRITIS-specific requirements are subject to the penalty framework for essential entities.

audit.description: Regular obligation to demonstrate IT security to the BSI per Section 39 BSIG
audit.name: Audit & Evidence
audit.empoweringIntro: Providing evidence is mandatory: as the operator of a critical installation you must demonstrate the implementation of your IT security measures to the BSI every three years (Section 39(1) BSIG). Structured audit preparation saves time and money and avoids findings.

bcm.description: Ensuring availability of critical services during crisis situations
bcm.name: Business Continuity
bcm.empoweringIntro: Your critical service must remain available even in a crisis. Well-considered business continuity management with tested emergency plans ensures that outages do not endanger security of supply.

bsiKontaktstelle.description: Registration with the BSI including current contact details per § 33 BSIG, and continuous reachability
bsiKontaktstelle.name: BSI Contact Point
bsiKontaktstelle.empoweringIntro: The BSI contact point is your interface to the Federal Office for Information Security. It must be reachable at all times so that the BSI can warn you about threats and you can report incidents within the deadlines.

lieferkette.description: Security requirements for suppliers and service providers of critical infrastructures
lieferkette.name: Supply Chain Security
lieferkette.empoweringIntro: Your IT security is only as strong as the weakest link in the supply chain. Operators of critical installations must ensure that suppliers and service providers also meet appropriate security standards — especially where they access critical systems.

physischeSicherheit.description: Protection of physical infrastructure and access controls for critical facilities
physischeSicherheit.name: Physical Security
physischeSicherheit.empoweringIntro: Critical installations need physical protection. Access controls, perimeter security and environmental monitoring prevent unauthorised entry and protect the availability of your infrastructure against physical threats.

risikomanagement.description: Systematic identification and assessment of risks for critical infrastructures per BSI-KritisV
risikomanagement.name: Risk Management
risikomanagement.empoweringIntro: Systematic risk management is the foundation of your critical infrastructure security. Only those who know their risks can implement appropriate state-of-the-art protection as required by Section 30 BSIG.

systemhaertung.description: Securing IT systems by minimizing attack surface and secure configuration
systemhaertung.name: System Hardening
systemhaertung.empoweringIntro: System hardening reduces the attack surface of your critical IT systems. Secure configuration, network segmentation and consistent patch management protect the availability of your infrastructure in line with the state of the art.

vorfallmanagement.description: Detection, reporting and handling of IT security incidents per §32 BSIG
vorfallmanagement.name: Incident Management
vorfallmanagement.empoweringIntro: Operators of critical installations must report security incidents to the BSI without undue delay. Structured incident management with clear escalation paths and rehearsed procedures is decisive for meeting reporting deadlines and minimising damage.

reasons.belowThreshold: BSI-KritisV threshold for this sector not reached
reasons.bsiDesignation: Designated as critical infrastructure operator by BSI (§ 10(1) BSIG)
reasons.essentialServiceCandidate: Potential operator of an essential service (Annex 1 BSIG)
reasons.sectorNotInScope: Sector is not covered by the scope of BSI-KritisV
reasons.thresholdExceeded: BSI-KritisV threshold for this sector exceeded — your organization qualifies as a KRITIS operator

auQ1.help: KRITIS operators must regularly demonstrate to the BSI that they take appropriate state-of-the-art precautions. The evidence is provided through security audits, reviews or certifications. The BSI has published guidance on evidence submissions that you should use as a basis.

maturity.level0: No evidence submission to the BSI established
maturity.level1: Evidence was submitted, but not on time or incomplete
maturity.level2: On-time submission with a documented process, individual findings
maturity.level3: Complete, on-time evidence submission with an established audit cycle and deficiency tracking

auQ1.title: Are the KRITIS compliance certificates submitted to the BSI on time every three years?
auQ1.tooltip: Under Section 39(1) BSIG, operators of critical facilities must demonstrate implementation of their measures every three years — the NIS2UmsG extended the cycle from two to three years. Where deficiencies are found, the BSI can demand a remediation plan.

auQ2.help: For the BSI evidence submission you need structured documentation describing all implemented technical and organisational measures. This includes ISMS policies, network plans, risk analyses, penetration test reports and training records. Without auditable documentation, the audit cannot be passed.

maturity.level0: No structured documentation of the IT security measures
maturity.level1: Partly documented, but not prepared in an auditable form
maturity.level2: Auditable documentation available for most areas
maturity.level3: Complete, audit-proof documentation with versioning and regular updates

auQ2.title: Is there auditable documentation of all IT security measures for the BSI evidence submission?
auQ2.tooltip: Under Section 39(1) BSIG, the compliance documentation must verifiably evidence the implemented measures. The BSI reviews the adequacy and completeness of the documentation.

auQ3.help: Internal audits are planned reviews of your IT security measures by your own or commissioned auditors. They should take place at least annually and cover all critical systems and processes. Identified deficiencies must be tracked and remedied before the official BSI evidence submission is due.

maturity.level0: No internal IT security audits
maturity.level1: Occasional ad hoc reviews without a fixed plan
maturity.level2: Regular internal audits with an audit plan, but deficiency follow-up is patchy
maturity.level3: Systematic internal audit programme with an annual plan, deficiency tracking and effectiveness checks

auQ3.title: Are internal audits of the critical IT systems carried out regularly?
auQ3.tooltip: Internal audits complement the BSI evidence obligation under Section 39(1) BSIG and help identify deficiencies before the official review. BSI module ISMS.1 requires regular internal reviews.

auQ4.help: After every audit — internal or external — the results should be analysed and turned into concrete improvement measures. This includes prioritising the findings, assigning owners and deadlines, and tracking implementation. In follow-up reviews, the BSI expects earlier deficiencies to have been remedied.

maturity.level0: No systematic processing of audit results
maturity.level1: Audit results are noted, but not followed up in a structured way
maturity.level2: An action plan is created, but implementation is only partly tracked
maturity.level3: Full PDCA cycle: findings are prioritised, measures implemented, effectiveness verified and documented

auQ4.title: Are findings from BSI reviews and external audits systematically turned into improvement measures?
auQ4.tooltip: Under Section 39(1) BSIG, the BSI can order specific measures where deficiencies are found. A structured improvement process (PDCA) ensures that findings are remedied sustainably.

bcmQ1.help: A BCMS defines how your organisation ensures the availability of the critical service even during serious disruptions. It covers business impact analyses (BIA), contingency plans, restart concepts and regular tests. For KRITIS operators this is particularly important, as outages can endanger the security of supply for the population.

maturity.level0: No BCMS in place, no contingency plans for the critical service
maturity.level1: Individual emergency measures defined, but no systematic BCMS
maturity.level2: BCMS established with BIA and contingency plans, but not tested regularly
maturity.level3: Complete BCMS in line with BSI 200-4 or ISO 22301 with regular tests and continuous improvement

bcmQ1.title: Does a business continuity management system (BCMS) exist for the critical service?
bcmQ1.tooltip: Section 30(1) BSIG requires measures to maintain the availability of critical services. A BCMS in line with BSI Standard 200-4 or ISO 22301 provides the organisational framework.

bcmQ2.help: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines the maximum downtime, RPO (Recovery Point Objective) the maximum data loss. For KRITIS operators this means: how long may your critical service (e.g. water supply, power generation, hospital operations) be down at most without endangering the security of supply? These values determine your entire contingency strategy.

maturity.level0: No RTO/RPO values defined
maturity.level1: Rough estimates exist, but not based on a BIA
maturity.level2: BIA carried out with documented RTO/RPO values for important systems
maturity.level3: Comprehensive BIA with validated RTO/RPO values, updated regularly and integrated into restart plans

bcmQ2.title: Have the maximum tolerable downtimes (RTO/RPO) been defined for your critical service?
bcmQ2.tooltip: The business impact analysis (BIA) is a core component of a BCMS under BSI Standard 200-4. It determines recovery time objectives (RTO) and tolerable data loss (RPO) for the critical service.

bcmQ3.help: Contingency plans that have never been tested almost always fail in a real emergency. KRITIS operators should run emergency exercises at least annually — from tabletop exercises (simulations) to technical failover tests. These verify whether the defined RTO/RPO values are met and whether staff know the procedures.

maturity.level0: No emergency exercises carried out
maturity.level1: Occasional tests, but not regular and without structured evaluation
maturity.level2: Annual exercises with documented results, but not all scenarios covered
maturity.level3: Regular exercise programme with different scenarios, documented evaluation and improvement measures

bcmQ3.title: Are contingency and restart plans regularly tested through exercises?
bcmQ3.tooltip: Section 30(1) BSIG requires appropriate precautions, which includes testing the contingency plans. BSI module DER.4 describes requirements for emergency exercises.

bcmQ4.help: Critical services require technical redundancies so that a single failure (e.g. data centre, network connection, power supply) does not lead to a total outage. This can include geo-redundancy, UPS systems, emergency power, mirrored databases or alternate sites. The redundancy strategy must match the defined RTO/RPO values.

maturity.level0: No technical redundancy for critical systems
maturity.level1: Individual redundancies exist (e.g. UPS), but no consistent strategy
maturity.level2: Important systems designed redundantly, fallback concept in place but not fully tested
maturity.level3: Consistent redundancy strategy with geo-redundant sites, regularly tested failover scenarios and documented recovery time

bcmQ4.title: Are redundant systems and alternate sites in place for the critical service?
bcmQ4.tooltip: Technical redundancy is an essential part of the BCMS for KRITIS operators. Section 30(1) BSIG requires state-of-the-art measures to ensure availability.

bsiQ1.help: The BSI contact point is the official interface between your company and the BSI. It must be registered with the BSI by name including contact details. The BSI uses this contact point to inform you about threat situations, vulnerabilities and security warnings. Without a registered contact point you cannot receive important warnings in time.

maturity.level0: No BSI contact point established or registered with the BSI
maturity.level1: Contact point designated, but not yet formally registered with the BSI
maturity.level2: Contact point registered with the BSI, but availability not consistently ensured
maturity.level3: Contact point registered with the BSI, reachable 24/7, with a documented deputisation arrangement and regular updates of the contact details

bsiQ1.title: Is your BSI contact point established and registered with the BSI by name?
bsiQ1.tooltip: Section 33 BSIG requires registration with the BSI including address and up-to-date contact details. For the BSI to reach you in acute threat situations, a designated unit must reliably receive these notifications.

bsiQ2.help: The BSI can send critical warnings at any time of day or night — e.g. during active cyberattacks on KRITIS sectors. Your contact point must therefore be reachable 24/7, for instance via an on-call phone, a staffed control centre or an on-call service. An email address staffed only on weekdays is not sufficient.

maturity.level0: No availability outside business hours
maturity.level1: Availability only during business hours, no on-call duty
maturity.level2: On-call duty established, but not covering all times without gaps
maturity.level3: 24/7 availability through an on-call service or control centre with defined response times and escalation paths

bsiQ2.title: Is the BSI contact point reachable around the clock (24/7)?
bsiQ2.tooltip: The contact details registered under Section 33 BSIG must be current and reachable. The BSI also issues warnings about acute threats outside business hours — a continuously staffed or on-call unit is the practical prerequisite.

bsiQ3.help: The BSI regularly sends situation reports, warnings and sector-specific information to KRITIS operators. Your contact point must not only receive this information but also assess it and forward it to the responsible departments (e.g. IT security, operations). This requires a defined process with clear responsibilities and response times.

maturity.level0: BSI notifications are not evaluated systematically
maturity.level1: Notifications are read, but not forwarded in a structured way
maturity.level2: Defined process for evaluation and forwarding, but response times not specified
maturity.level3: Structured process with defined response times, an assessment matrix and follow-up of the measures initiated
