bsiQ3.title: Are BSI warnings and situation reports evaluated promptly and forwarded to the responsible units?
bsiQ3.tooltip: The contact point must not only receive BSI information but also be able to evaluate and route it internally. Mere registration under Section 33 BSIG is not sufficient for this.

bsiQ4.help: The BSI organises sector-specific and cross-sector KRITIS exercises (e.g. LÜKEX) in which cooperation between the BSI and operators in a crisis is rehearsed. Your contact point's participation in such exercises improves responsiveness and provides valuable insights into weaknesses in the reporting processes.

maturity.level0: No participation in KRITIS exercises
maturity.level1: Willingness in principle, but no participation yet
maturity.level2: Participation in individual exercises; findings are documented
maturity.level3: Regular participation in BSI exercises and own exercises with the contact point, documented lessons learned and process improvements

bsiQ4.title: Is the contact point regularly involved in BSI KRITIS exercises?
bsiQ4.tooltip: The BSI conducts and participates in cross-sector exercises. Taking part strengthens cooperation and tests the reporting channels. BSI module DER.2.1 recommends regular exercises.

lkQ1.help: As a KRITIS operator, you bear responsibility for the IT security of your critical service — even where parts of it are outsourced. Contracts with suppliers and IT service providers must therefore set out specific security requirements: patch management, incident response, access controls, audit rights and reporting duties for security incidents.

maturity.level0: No IT security requirements in supplier contracts
maturity.level1: General security clauses in individual contracts, but not standardised
maturity.level2: Standardised security requirements in most contracts, including audit rights
maturity.level3: Comprehensive security requirements in all relevant contracts with SLAs, audit rights, reporting duties and termination rights in case of security deficiencies

lkQ1.title: Are security-relevant requirements anchored in contracts with suppliers and IT service providers?
lkQ1.tooltip: Section 30(1) BSIG requires appropriate precautions in the supply chain as well. BSI module ORP.1 describes requirements for contract design with external service providers.

lkQ2.help: You should have an overview of which suppliers and service providers have access to your critical systems or are relevant to their operation. They should be assessed regularly with regard to their IT security — e.g. through questionnaires, certification evidence (ISO 27001), audit reports or on-site reviews.

maturity.level0: No assessment of suppliers' IT security
maturity.level1: Occasional reviews, but no systematic process
maturity.level2: Regular assessment of the most important suppliers based on defined criteria
maturity.level3: Systematic supplier risk management with classification, regular assessment, an audit programme and follow-up of measures

lkQ2.title: Are critical suppliers and service providers assessed with regard to their IT security?
lkQ2.tooltip: Assessing supply chain security is part of the risk analysis under Section 30(1) BSIG. BSI module OPS.1.1.3 describes requirements for outsourcing management.

lkQ3.help: If a critical IT service provider fails — whether through a cyberattack of its own, insolvency or contract termination — your critical service must still keep running. This requires contingency plans: alternative providers, in-house fallback solutions, documented handover processes and regularly updated exit strategies.

maturity.level0: No contingency planning for supplier failures
maturity.level1: Critical dependencies known, but no documented contingency plans
maturity.level2: Contingency plans for the most important suppliers in place, alternative service providers identified
maturity.level3: Comprehensive contingency plans with tested exit strategies, alternative service providers and regular review of dependencies

lkQ3.title: Are there contingency plans for the failure of critical suppliers or service providers?
lkQ3.tooltip: Dependence on third parties must be taken into account in the BCM (Section 30(1) BSIG). BSI Standard 200-4 requires considering external dependencies in the business impact analysis.

lkQ4.help: Contractually agreed security requirements are only effective if compliance is actually verified. This can be done through regular audits, obtaining current certifications, providers' security reports or technical checks (e.g. vulnerability scans of interfaces). Close monitoring is particularly necessary for providers with remote access to critical systems.

maturity.level0: No review of security requirements at suppliers
maturity.level1: Occasional review of individual suppliers, but not systematic
maturity.level2: Regular review of the most important suppliers based on defined audit criteria
maturity.level3: Systematic audit programme for all critical suppliers with documented results, follow-up of measures and an escalation process

lkQ4.title: Is supplier compliance with the security requirements reviewed regularly?
lkQ4.tooltip: Ongoing monitoring of supply chain security is part of the evidence obligation under Section 39(1) BSIG. The BSI can also review the adequacy of measures with regard to the supply chain.

psQ1.help: Server rooms, control rooms and other areas housing critical IT infrastructure must be protected against unauthorised entry. An access control system can include electronic badges, biometric systems or key management. Logging of all entries and regular review of access authorisations are essential.

maturity.level0: No access control for critical IT areas
maturity.level1: Simple key allocation without logging or systematic administration
maturity.level2: Electronic access control system with logging, but authorisations not reviewed regularly
maturity.level3: Multi-level access control system with electronic logging, regular authorisation reviews and visitor rules

psQ1.title: Does a physical access control system exist for the areas housing critical IT infrastructure?
psQ1.tooltip: Section 30(1) BSIG requires appropriate precautions including physical security. BSI modules INF.1 (general building) and INF.2 (data centre) describe specific requirements for access controls.

psQ2.help: Physical threats such as fire, water ingress, power failure or extreme temperatures can destroy critical IT systems. KRITIS operators must take appropriate protective measures: fire alarm and extinguishing systems, water detectors, uninterruptible power supply (UPS), emergency power (generator), air conditioning and lightning protection.

maturity.level0: No systematic protection against environmental influences and natural hazards
maturity.level1: Basic fire protection in place, but no comprehensive hazard analysis
maturity.level2: Protective measures against the main hazards implemented (fire, power, climate), regularly maintained
maturity.level3: Comprehensive protection in line with EN 50600 or comparable, with redundant UPS/emergency generator, extinguishing system, climate monitoring and regular function tests

psQ2.title: Are the buildings and facilities housing critical infrastructure protected against environmental influences and natural hazards?
psQ2.tooltip: BSI module INF.1 requires protecting buildings against environmental hazards such as fire, water, lightning and power failure. For data centres, INF.2 imposes elevated requirements.

psQ3.help: In addition to access control, critical facilities should be protected by further physical security measures: video surveillance at entrances and sensitive areas, an intrusion alarm system connected to a control centre, perimeter protection (fences, barriers) and site lighting. The scope depends on the threat situation and the facility's protection needs.

maturity.level0: No supplementary physical security measures
maturity.level1: Individual measures in place (e.g. camera surveillance), but not comprehensive
maturity.level2: Video surveillance and intrusion alarm system at critical areas, connected to a control centre
maturity.level3: Comprehensive perimeter protection with video surveillance, intrusion alarms, physical barriers, control centre connection and regular security walkthroughs

psQ3.title: Is physical security supplemented by video surveillance, intrusion detection systems or perimeter protection?
psQ3.tooltip: For KRITIS facilities with elevated protection needs, Section 30(1) BSIG requires state-of-the-art measures. BSI module INF.1 recommends supplementary monitoring measures for critical areas.

rmQ1.help: KRITIS operators must systematically determine which risks endanger the availability, integrity, authenticity and confidentiality of their critical service. The risk analysis should cover all IT systems necessary for providing the critical service. The BSI recommends the methodology of BSI Standard 200-3 as a basis.

maturity.level0: No systematic risk analysis carried out for the critical service
maturity.level1: Rough risk estimate exists, but not methodically sound or documented
maturity.level2: Documented risk analysis using a recognised methodology, but not updated regularly
maturity.level3: Regularly updated risk analysis in line with BSI Standard 200-3 or ISO 27005 with full coverage of all critical systems

rmQ1.title: Have you carried out a systematic state-of-the-art risk analysis for your critical service?
rmQ1.tooltip: Section 30(1) BSIG requires appropriate organisational and technical precautions in line with the state of the art. A risk analysis based on BSI Standard 200-3 or ISO 27005 provides the foundation.

rmQ2.help: An ISMS forms the organisational framework for your entire IT security. It defines responsibilities, policies, processes and controls. For KRITIS operators, an ISMS based on ISO 27001 or BSI IT-Grundschutz is the most efficient way to demonstrably implement the requirements of Section 30 BSIG. The scope must cover at least all IT systems of the critical service.

maturity.level0: No ISMS in place
maturity.level1: Individual security policies exist, but no systematic ISMS
maturity.level2: ISMS set up and operated, but not certified or with gaps in scope
maturity.level3: Certified ISMS according to ISO 27001 or BSI IT-Grundschutz with full KRITIS scope and regular re-certification

rmQ2.title: Is an information security management system (ISMS) established for the KRITIS scope?
rmQ2.tooltip: An ISMS based on ISO 27001 or BSI IT-Grundschutz is the recommended foundation for implementing Section 30 BSIG. BSI module ISMS.1 defines the minimum requirements.

rmQ3.help: Attack detection systems (SzA) comprise technical measures such as SIEM systems, IDS/IPS, log analysis and anomaly detection. In its guidance, the BSI distinguishes three areas: logging (collecting logs), detection (recognising attacks) and response (reacting to detected attacks). KRITIS operators must demonstrate the use of SzA as part of the BSI evidence obligation.

maturity.level0: No attack detection systems in use
maturity.level1: Basic log collection in place, but no systematic evaluation or detection
maturity.level2: SIEM or comparable system in use with detection rules, but response processes not fully defined
maturity.level3: Full SzA implementation in line with the BSI guidance: central logging, automated detection, defined response processes and 24/7 monitoring

rmQ3.title: Are attack detection systems (SzA) in use as required by Section 31 BSIG?
rmQ3.tooltip: Section 31 BSIG obliges KRITIS operators to use attack detection systems (SzA). The BSI has published guidance on SzA describing specific requirements for logging, detection and response.

rmQ4.help: A treatment strategy must be defined for every identified risk: reduce the risk (implement a measure), transfer it (e.g. cyber insurance), avoid it (shut down the system) or accept it (a conscious decision for low risks). The implemented measures must be regularly reviewed for effectiveness — a formal risk acceptance process with management involvement is required.

maturity.level0: No systematic risk treatment
maturity.level1: Individual measures are implemented, but without a documented treatment plan
maturity.level2: Documented risk treatment plans for the most important risks; effectiveness is checked occasionally
maturity.level3: Complete risk treatment process with management involvement, regular effectiveness reviews and KPI-based success measurement

rmQ4.title: Are identified risks treated systematically and is the effectiveness of the measures reviewed?
rmQ4.tooltip: Risk treatment and effectiveness reviews are core components of the ISMS under BSI module ISMS.1. Section 30(1) BSIG requires appropriate precautions whose adequacy must be reviewed regularly.

shQ1.help: System hardening means disabling unnecessary services, changing default passwords, applying security configurations and minimising the attack surface. For KRITIS systems you should use recognised hardening standards such as CIS Benchmarks, BSI recommendations or vendor-specific security guides. Hardening must be documented and applied to every new system.

maturity.level0: No systematic hardening of the IT systems
maturity.level1: Individual measures (e.g. default passwords changed), but no uniform standard
maturity.level2: Hardening guidelines defined and implemented for the most important systems; compliance checked occasionally
maturity.level3: Consistent hardening according to recognised standards (CIS/BSI) with automated compliance checks and deviation management

shQ1.title: Are IT systems within the KRITIS scope configured according to recognised hardening standards?
shQ1.tooltip: Section 30(1) BSIG requires state-of-the-art technical precautions. BSI module SYS.1.1 (general server) describes requirements for secure configuration. CIS Benchmarks and BSI hardening guidelines are recognised standards.

shQ2.help: Critical KRITIS systems (e.g. control technology, process control) must be separated at network level from less critical areas (e.g. office IT, internet). This prevents an attack on the office IT from spreading directly to the critical infrastructure. Segmentation is achieved through firewalls, VLANs, DMZs and dedicated networks for OT systems (operational technology).

maturity.level0: No network segmentation; critical and non-critical systems in the same network
maturity.level1: Basic segmentation exists (e.g. VLANs), but firewall rules are not restrictive
maturity.level2: Critical systems in separate segments with firewall rules; OT and IT fundamentally separated
maturity.level3: Multi-layer segmentation with dedicated security zones, strict firewall rules, IDS/IPS at zone transitions and regular review of the rule sets

shQ2.title: Is the network infrastructure segmented to separate critical systems from other network areas?
shQ2.tooltip: Network segmentation is a core measure under Section 30(1) BSIG. BSI module NET.1.1 (network architecture and design) requires separating network segments by protection needs.

shQ3.help: Unpatched vulnerabilities are one of the most common entry points for cyberattacks. KRITIS operators must have a structured process for promptly assessing and applying security updates. For OT systems (control technology, SCADA), patching must be planned carefully, as outages of the critical service must be avoided. A risk assessment process helps weigh urgency against availability.

maturity.level0: No structured patch management; updates are not applied regularly
maturity.level1: Patches are applied occasionally, but without a defined process or prioritisation
maturity.level2: Defined patch process with prioritisation by criticality, but not all systems covered (e.g. OT missing)
maturity.level3: Comprehensive patch management for IT and OT with risk assessment, defined maintenance windows, a test environment and rollback procedures

shQ3.title: Are security updates and patches for critical systems applied promptly and according to a defined process?
shQ3.tooltip: Patch management is a basic requirement under Section 30(1) BSIG (state of the art). BSI module OPS.1.1.3 describes requirements for patch and change management. Special requirements apply to OT systems.

vmQ1.help: KRITIS operators must have a clearly defined process describing: how are incidents detected (e.g. through SzA, helpdesk reports, automatic alarms)? How are they assessed (severity, impact on the critical service)? When and how is the BSI informed? Who is responsible internally? Without a documented process, valuable minutes are lost in an emergency.

maturity.level0: No documented incident response process in place
maturity.level1: Informal arrangements for incident handling, but not documented
maturity.level2: Documented process with roles, escalation levels and BSI reporting channel, but not practised regularly
maturity.level3: Fully documented and regularly practised incident response process with defined escalation levels, BSI reporting channel and follow-up

vmQ1.title: Is there a documented process for detecting, assessing and reporting IT security incidents?
vmQ1.tooltip: Section 32 BSIG obliges KRITIS operators to report significant IT disruptions to the BSI without undue delay. BSI module DER.2.1 describes requirements for handling security incidents.

vmQ2.help: In the event of a significant IT disruption you must inform the BSI without undue delay — submit an initial report at the latest within 24 hours, a follow-up report with an assessment within 72 hours and a final report within one month. This requires: prepared reporting forms, clear criteria for 'significant disruption', a designated reporter and tested reporting channels (BSI reporting platform).

maturity.level0: No preparation for BSI reporting obligations; reporting deadlines unknown
maturity.level1: Reporting deadlines known, but no prepared processes or forms
maturity.level2: Reporting process defined with templates and responsibilities, but not yet tested in a real case
maturity.level3: Fully established reporting process with pre-filled forms, tested reporting channels, defined criteria and regular exercises

vmQ2.title: Can you meet the BSI reporting deadlines for significant IT disruptions (without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours)?
vmQ2.tooltip: Section 32 BSIG requires significant security incidents to be reported to the BSI without undue delay. The staggered deadlines — initial report within 24 hours, report within 72 hours, final report no later than one month afterwards — must be met.

vmQ3.help: A structured follow-up should take place after every security incident: what happened? How was the incident detected? Was the response appropriate? Which vulnerabilities were exploited? Which measures will prevent a recurrence? The results feed into improving the security measures. The BSI final report under Section 32 BSIG requires exactly this analysis.

maturity.level0: No systematic follow-up of security incidents
maturity.level1: Occasional informal evaluation after serious incidents
maturity.level2: Structured post-incident reviews for significant incidents with documented findings
maturity.level3: Systematic follow-up of all incidents with root cause analysis, documented improvement measures and effectiveness checks

vmQ3.title: Are IT security incidents systematically followed up and improvements derived from them?
vmQ3.tooltip: Follow-up (lessons learned) is an essential part of incident management under BSI module DER.2.3. Section 32(1) no. 4 BSIG requires final reports that also describe causes and countermeasures.

vmQ4.help: A CSIRT or incident response team consists of specialists who handle the technical analysis, containment and clean-up of serious IT security incidents. KRITIS operators should either build their own team or have a specialised provider under contract that supports them within defined response times in an emergency. The team should have communication channels coordinated with the contact point and the BSI.

maturity.level0: No incident response team in place or commissioned
maturity.level1: IT staff handle incidents ad hoc; no specialised IR capacity
maturity.level2: External IR provider under contract with defined response times, but internal processes not fully integrated
maturity.level3: In-house or commissioned CSIRT with defined response times, regular exercises, forensic capabilities and coordinated communication channels with the BSI

vmQ4.title: Is a KRITIS-specific Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) established or commissioned?
vmQ4.tooltip: For KRITIS operators, the BSI recommends establishing or commissioning a specialised incident response team. BSI modules DER.2.1 and DER.2.2 describe requirements for incident handling and forensic analysis.

q1.description: Section 33 BSIG requires registration with the BSI including current contact details. A reachable contact point is the basic prerequisite for warnings and queries to arrive.
q1.title: Have you registered a contact point with the BSI, and is it reachable 24/7?

q2.description: Section 30 BSIG requires appropriate precautions based on a risk assessment — including the IT systems, components and processes of the critical service.
q2.title: Do you carry out regular risk analyses for your critical supply processes?

q3.description: Section 32 BSIG: significant disruptions of the critical service must be reported to the BSI without undue delay — with classification and initial assessment.
q3.title: Is there a process for reporting significant IT disruptions to the BSI?

q4.description: Business continuity management according to BSI Standard 200-4: contingency plans must be documented, tested and updated regularly.
q4.title: Have you tested contingency plans for the failure of your critical infrastructure?

q5.description: Supply chain security under Section 30 BSIG: critical dependencies on suppliers must be identified and their security measures contractually secured.
q5.title: Do you review the IT security of the suppliers of your critical services?

q6.description: Section 39(1) BSIG: every three years, operators of critical facilities must demonstrate implementation through security audits, reviews or certifications.
q6.title: Can you demonstrate the implementation of your security measures to the BSI?

q7.description: Physical security covers access control systems, perimeter protection, surveillance and protection against environmental hazards (fire, water, power).
q7.title: Are your critical facilities protected against unauthorised physical access?

q8.description: Section 30 BSIG: system hardening according to the state of the art — e.g. via BSI IT-Grundschutz or ISO 27001, with patch management and secure configuration.
q8.title: Are the IT systems of your critical infrastructure hardened according to the state of the art?

au1.description: Prepare for the mandatory review of IT security measures under Section 39(1) BSIG. Every three years, operators of critical facilities must demonstrate compliance through security audits, reviews or certifications.
au1.firstStep: Find out about recognised audit bodies (e.g. via the BSI portal) and request offers for a Section 39 audit.
au1.title: Prepare for the audit under Section 39 BSIG

au2.description: Implement a regular internal audit programme to identify weaknesses early and support preparation for the external evidence submissions under Section 39(1) BSIG.
au2.firstStep: Schedule semi-annual internal IT security audits and train internal auditors in the requirements of the BSI-KritisV.
au2.title: Establish an internal audit programme

au3.checklist:
Create audit plan per §39 BSIG
Plan internal and external audits
Prepare evidence documentation
au3.description: Use technical tools for continuous monitoring of IT security compliance (e.g. SIEM, vulnerability scanners, configuration management) in line with Section 39(1) BSIG. This eases audits and reduces risks.
au3.firstStep: Implement a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system for central logging and anomaly detection.
au3.title: Build continuous compliance monitoring

bcm1.description: Identify all business-critical processes and IT systems and assess the impact of outages under Section 30(1) BSIG. This is the foundation for contingency and recovery plans.
bcm1.firstStep: Create a list of all core processes and assess for each: maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
bcm1.title: Carry out a business impact analysis for critical services

bcm2.description: Develop detailed plans for maintaining or rapidly restoring critical services under Section 30(1) BSIG. This includes technical redundancies, alternate sites and manual emergency procedures.
bcm2.firstStep: Document a step-by-step recovery plan for your most critical IT system, including responsibilities and contacts.
bcm2.title: Develop contingency and recovery plans

bcm3.checklist:
Conduct Business Impact Analysis
Develop and document BCM strategy
Test and update emergency plans
bcm3.description: Test your contingency plans through regular exercises (tabletop exercises, technical tests, full-scale exercises) under Section 30(1) BSIG. Only tested plans work in a real emergency.
bcm3.firstStep: Plan a tabletop exercise with a simulated ransomware attack and involve all relevant stakeholders (IT, management, communications).
bcm3.title: Carry out regular BCM exercises and tests

bsi1.description: Register your organisation with the BSI and designate a dedicated contact point. Section 33 BSIG requires an address and current contact details; changes must be notified to the BSI.
bsi1.firstStep: Register your company on the BSI web portal and designate a contact person with name, role and availability (24/7).
bsi1.title: Set up registration and contact point under Section 33 BSIG

bsi2.description: Regularly verify that the communication channels to the BSI (email, phone, web portal) are working, in line with Section 33 BSIG. In an emergency, disruptions and security incidents must be reportable without delay.
bsi2.firstStep: Carry out a test reporting procedure via the BSI web portal to verify credentials and the process.
bsi2.title: Test and document the BSI reporting channels

bsi3.checklist:
Designate BSI contact point (§ 33 BSIG)
Document communication channels to BSI
Define reporting obligations and deadlines
bsi3.description: Create a structured communication plan for the exchange of information with the BSI under Section 33 BSIG (registration) and Section 32 BSIG (reporting obligations). This covers incident reporting duties, participation in situation reports and receiving warnings.
bsi3.firstStep: Subscribe to BSI warnings and CERT-Bund advisories and define internal escalation paths for BSI information.
bsi3.title: Develop a communication plan with the BSI

lk1.description: Record all external service providers and suppliers necessary for operating your critical infrastructure (Section 30(1) BSIG). This includes IT service providers, cloud providers, maintenance firms and hardware suppliers.
lk1.firstStep: Create a spreadsheet of all IT service providers and assess their criticality for your KRITIS service.
lk1.title: Inventory critical suppliers and service providers

lk2.description: Ensure that all contracts with critical suppliers contain security requirements, audit rights and reporting duties for security incidents (Section 30(1) BSIG).
lk2.firstStep: Develop a contract clause template with IT security requirements (e.g. ISO 27001 certification, patch management SLA).
lk2.title: Include security requirements in supplier contracts

lk3.checklist:
Define supplier assessment criteria
Include security requirements in contracts
Regular review of suppliers
lk3.description: Regularly assess the IT security of your critical suppliers through audits, questionnaires or certificate checks under Section 30(1) BSIG. Supply chain attacks are a growing threat.
lk3.firstStep: Request current ISO 27001 or TISAX certificates from your top 5 suppliers.
lk3.title: Carry out regular supplier security assessments

ps1.description: Secure all critical IT and OT rooms (server rooms, control centres, network equipment) with physical access controls such as chip cards, biometric systems or keys under Section 30(1) BSIG.
ps1.firstStep: Walk through all technical rooms and check whether access controls are in place and working.
ps1.title: Implement physical access controls for critical infrastructure

ps2.description: Protect critical IT infrastructure against physical threats such as fire, flooding and power failure through appropriate measures (e.g. fire alarm system, UPS, air conditioning) under Section 30(1) BSIG.
ps2.firstStep: Check whether your data centre has an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) and an emergency generator.
ps2.title: Environmental security against fire, water and power failure

ps3.checklist:
Implement access controls for server rooms
Video surveillance for critical areas
Visitor registration and escort policy
ps3.description: Develop a holistic physical security concept under Section 30(1) BSIG covering perimeter protection, access controls, video surveillance, visitor management and alerting.
ps3.firstStep: Commission a security consultancy or use BSI standards (e.g. IT-Grundschutz module INF.1 or the data centre module).
ps3.title: Create a comprehensive physical security concept

rm1.description: Implement a systematic method for identifying and assessing IT risks to your critical services under Section 30(1) BSIG. The analysis must be updated regularly.
rm1.firstStep: Choose a recognised risk analysis method (e.g. BSI Standard 200-3, ISO 27005) and schedule a kick-off meeting.
rm1.title: Establish an IT risk analysis methodology under Section 30 BSIG

rm2.description: Assess all identified IT risks (likelihood × impact) and derive prioritised risk mitigation measures, as required by Section 30(1) BSIG.
rm2.firstStep: Create a risk register with all identified threats, their assessment and the status of countermeasures.
rm2.title: Develop a risk assessment and action plan

rm3.checklist:
Define risk assessment methodology
Identify critical business processes
Prioritize risks and derive measures
rm3.description: Establish a process for continuously monitoring and re-assessing IT risks under Section 30(1) BSIG. New threats (e.g. zero-day exploits) or changes in the IT landscape must be captured promptly.
rm3.firstStep: Set up a quarterly risk review meeting in which the risk register is updated and new threats are assessed.
rm3.title: Introduce continuous risk monitoring

sh1.description: Harden all critical servers and endpoints by disabling unnecessary services, applying secure configuration and restrictive permissions under Section 30(1) BSIG. This considerably reduces the attack surface.
sh1.firstStep: Use CIS Benchmarks or BSI SiSyPHuS guidelines to define a baseline hardening configuration for Windows/Linux servers.
sh1.title: Server and endpoint hardening according to the state of the art

sh2.description: Segment your network by criticality and protection needs (e.g. OT vs office IT) and enforce restrictive firewall rules (Section 30(1) BSIG). This limits the spread of attacks.
sh2.firstStep: Create a network zone architecture (e.g. DMZ, production network, office network) and document permitted data flows.
sh2.title: Implement network segmentation and firewall rules

sh3.checklist:
Define baseline hardening guidelines
Introduce configuration management
Establish patch management process
sh3.description: Develop standardised hardening guidelines for all system types (servers, clients, network devices, OT components) under Section 30(1) BSIG and enforce them through configuration management.
sh3.firstStep: Use tools such as the Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit or Ansible/Puppet to roll out hardening configurations automatically.
sh3.title: Develop comprehensive hardening baselines

vm1.description: Develop a comprehensive contingency plan for IT security incidents in critical infrastructure under Section 32 BSIG. The plan must cover detection, assessment, containment, reporting to the BSI and recovery.
vm1.firstStep: Carry out a business impact analysis to identify the most critical IT systems and their maximum tolerable downtimes.
vm1.title: Create an IT emergency management plan for KRITIS services

vm2.description: Define clear criteria for assessing and classifying IT security incidents under Section 32 BSIG. This determines whether an incident is significant and must be reported to the BSI.
vm2.firstStep: Create a table with severity levels (e.g. 1-5) and concrete examples for each level (e.g. 'outage >30 min = level 4').
vm2.title: Implement an incident classification system

vm3.checklist:
Create IT emergency management plan
Implement reporting process per §32 BSIG
Conduct regular emergency exercises
vm3.description: After every relevant IT security incident, hold a structured debrief to identify weaknesses and derive preventive measures (Section 32 BSIG).
vm3.firstStep: Create a template for post-incident reviews with questions such as: What happened? Why? What went well? What must be improved?
vm3.title: Establish a lessons-learned process after incidents

dora.name: DORA
dora.description: Digital operational resilience for the financial sector

drittanbieter.description: Management of risks from ICT third-party service providers per Art. 28-44 DORA
drittanbieter.name: ICT Third-Party Risk Management
drittanbieter.empoweringIntro: ICT third-party providers are a central part of the digital value chain in the financial sector. DORA requires financial entities to systematically identify, assess and contractually safeguard all risks arising from the use of ICT third-party services. The following questions check whether your organisation meets the ICT third-party risk management requirements of Articles 28–44 DORA.

governance.description: Management responsibility and proportional DORA implementation (Art. 4-6 DORA)
governance.name: Governance & Proportionality
governance.empoweringIntro: DORA requires the management body to bear overall responsibility for digital operational resilience. Management must approve and oversee the ICT risk management framework and be kept regularly informed about ICT risks. The following questions check whether your organisation implements the governance requirements of Articles 4–6 DORA, including the proportionality principle.

ictRisikomanagement.description: Framework for ICT risk management per Art. 5-16 DORA
ictRisikomanagement.name: ICT Risk Management
ictRisikomanagement.empoweringIntro: ICT risk management is the foundation of digital operational resilience. DORA obliges financial entities to establish a comprehensive framework covering identification, protection, detection, response and recovery. The following questions check whether your organisation meets the core requirements of Articles 5–16 DORA.

informationsaustausch.description: Arrangements for sharing information on cyber threats per Art. 45 DORA
informationsaustausch.name: Information Sharing
informationsaustausch.empoweringIntro: Sharing information about cyber threats between financial entities is an essential element of the sector’s collective resilience. Article 45 DORA enables and encourages the voluntary exchange of threat indicators, tactical information and early warnings. The following questions check whether your organisation takes an active part in information sharing and has created suitable structures for it.

resilienceTesting.description: Regular testing of digital operational resilience (Art. 24-27 DORA)
resilienceTesting.name: Resilience Testing
resilienceTesting.empoweringIntro: Digital operational resilience testing ensures that financial entities regularly examine their ICT systems and processes for vulnerabilities and robustness. DORA distinguishes between general testing (Articles 24–25) and advanced threat-led penetration testing (TLPT, Articles 26–27). The following questions assess your maturity in conducting resilience tests.

vorfallmanagement.description: Classification, reporting and management of ICT-related incidents per Art. 17-23 DORA
vorfallmanagement.name: ICT Incident Management
vorfallmanagement.empoweringIntro: Effective ICT incident management is decisive for limiting damage and restoring business operations quickly. DORA defines uniform requirements for detecting, classifying, reporting and following up ICT-related incidents. The following questions check whether your organisation fully implements Articles 17–23 DORA.

proportionality.criticalIctNoSimplification: No simplification — critical ICT functions require full compliance
proportionality.ictProviderContractual: Contractual requirements depending on significance of ICT service
proportionality.microSimplified: Simplified ICT risk management per Art. 16 DORA
proportionality.smallProportional: Proportional requirements according to size and risk profile

reasons.criticalIctProvider: Critical ICT third-party service provider (Art. 31 DORA) — oversight framework applicable
reasons.directlyRegulated: Directly regulated financial entity per Art. 2(1) DORA
reasons.directlyRegulatedMicro: Directly regulated micro-enterprise — simplified requirements (Art. 16 DORA)
reasons.directlyRegulatedSignificant: Directly regulated significant financial entity — full DORA requirements
reasons.directlyRegulatedSmall: Directly regulated small entity — proportional requirements
reasons.ictProvider: ICT third-party service provider — contractual requirements per Art. 28-30 DORA
reasons.notInScope: Not within DORA scope — not a regulated financial entity
reasons.otherFinancialNotCovered: Financial entity outside DORA scope per Art. 2(3)

tisax.name: TISAX
tisax.description: Information security in the automotive industry

betriebssicherheit.description: Secure operational processes incl. change management and monitoring
betriebssicherheit.name: Operations Security
betriebssicherheit.empoweringIntro: Stable operation, secure processes: well-designed operational processes with change management and monitoring safeguard the availability and integrity of your IT systems.

compliance.description: Compliance with legal and contractual requirements
compliance.name: Compliance
compliance.empoweringIntro: Improve continuously: regular audits and management reviews ensure that your information security exists in practice, not just on paper.

datenschutz.description: Protection of personal data in the automotive environment
datenschutz.name: Data Protection
datenschutz.empoweringIntro: Data protection as a competitive advantage: meeting GDPR requirements in the automotive context strengthens your position as a trustworthy partner to the OEMs.

kommunikation.description: Protection of information in networks and during transmission
kommunikation.name: Communications Security
kommunikation.empoweringIntro: Secure channels: encrypted transmission and controlled information exchange prevent confidential data from ending up in the wrong hands.

kryptografie.description: Use of cryptographic measures to protect information
kryptografie.name: Cryptography
kryptografie.empoweringIntro: Encrypt data effectively: strong cryptography in transit and at rest protects confidential information even in the event of a security incident.

lieferanten.description: Security requirements for suppliers and their monitoring
lieferanten.name: Supplier Management
lieferanten.empoweringIntro: Security in the supply chain: as an automotive supplier you must ensure that your subcontractors also meet the TISAX requirements.

organisation.description: Establishing and maintaining an ISMS per VDA ISA / ISO 27001
organisation.name: Information Security Organization
organisation.empoweringIntro: Security starts with leadership: a clear information security policy with defined responsibilities is the foundation for all further TISAX measures.

personal.description: Security checks, training and awareness of employees
personal.name: Human Resource Security
personal.empoweringIntro: People make the difference: trained and aware employees recognise threats faster and act security-consciously — the best protection against social engineering.

physischeSicherheit.description: Physical protection of buildings, server rooms and work areas
physischeSicherheit.name: Physical Security
physischeSicherheit.empoweringIntro: Control entry, protect assets: defined security zones and consistent access controls prevent unauthorised persons from reaching confidential information.

prototypenschutz.description: Special measures for protecting prototypes and pre-series vehicles
prototypenschutz.name: Prototype Protection
prototypenschutz.empoweringIntro: Preserve innovation: in the automotive industry, protecting prototypes and development data is business-critical — physical and digital measures must go hand in hand.

technologie.description: Secure configuration and operation of IT systems and networks
technologie.name: Technical Security
technologie.empoweringIntro: Technology as a shield: up-to-date endpoint security, network segmentation and systematic patch management keep your systems resilient against cyber attacks.

zugangskontrolle.description: Control and monitoring of access to IT systems and data
zugangskontrolle.name: Access Control
zugangskontrolle.empoweringIntro: Access only where warranted: a role-based authorisation concept with regular reviews protects sensitive OEM data from unauthorised access.

reasons.highDataSensitivity: High protection needs — TISAX Assessment Level 2 (plausibility check)
reasons.normalProtection: Normal protection needs — TISAX Assessment Level 1 (self-assessment)
reasons.notAutomotiveSupplier: Not an automotive industry supplier — TISAX not applicable
reasons.personalDataHandling: Processing of personal data — additional data protection requirements
reasons.prototypeHandling: Handling of prototypes — extended protection needs for prototype protection
reasons.veryHighDataSensitivity: Very high protection needs — TISAX Assessment Level 3 (comprehensive on-site audit)

bs1.description: Implement comprehensive malware protection for all automotive development and production systems per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.7. Take special requirements for OT environments into account.
bs1.firstStep: Deploy anti-malware solutions on all workstations and servers handling automotive data (development, PLM, MES).
bs1.title: Malware protection for automotive development environments

bs2.description: Establish vulnerability management for all automotive IT and OT systems per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.8. Prioritize patching for production-adjacent and prototype systems.
bs2.firstStep: Implement automated vulnerability scanning for all automotive systems (at least monthly for development environments).
bs2.title: Vulnerability management for automotive systems

comp1.description: Implement a comprehensive compliance framework to meet all VDA ISA/TISAX requirements per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.31. Prepare for a TISAX assessment.
comp1.firstStep: Conduct a TISAX gap assessment to identify deviations between the current state and VDA ISA requirements.
comp1.title: Implement a TISAX compliance framework

comp2.description: Conduct regular reviews to ensure compliance with all TISAX and automotive security requirements per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.36. Document evidence for audits.
comp2.firstStep: Schedule quarterly TISAX compliance reviews with defined checkpoints (VDA ISA controls, measure status).
comp2.title: Conduct regular compliance reviews

ds1.description: Implement a data protection management system for automotive-specific personal data (e.g., vehicle data, test drivers) per VDA ISA 6 (Data Protection module) and GDPR.
ds1.firstStep: Identify all processing activities involving automotive personal data and maintain a record of processing activities per Art. 30 GDPR.
ds1.title: Establish data protection management for automotive data

ds2.description: Conduct regular data protection audits and reviews, especially for automotive data processing activities (connected car, test data) per VDA ISA 6 (Data Protection module).
ds2.firstStep: Schedule an annual data protection audit focusing on automotive-specific data processing (e.g., telematics, test drives).
ds2.title: Conduct data protection audits and reviews

kom1.description: Implement comprehensive network security measures for automotive development networks (segmentation, firewalls, IDS/IPS) per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.20.
kom1.firstStep: Segment the network by sensitivity level (e.g., prototype zone, development, production, office) with strict firewall controls.
kom1.title: Network security for automotive development networks

kom2.description: Implement encrypted transmission channels for all automotive-sensitive data (internal and external to suppliers/OEMs) per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.14.
kom2.firstStep: Define secure transmission methods for prototype data (e.g., SFTP, HTTPS, VPN) and prohibit unencrypted channels.
kom2.title: Secure data transmission for automotive information

kry1.description: Develop an enterprise-wide cryptography concept for automotive data at rest and in transit per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.24. Define encryption standards for prototype information.
kry1.firstStep: Create a cryptography concept with defined algorithms, key lengths, and use cases (e.g., AES-256 for prototype data).
kry1.title: Develop a cryptography concept for automotive data

kry2.description: Implement secure key management for all cryptographic keys in automotive applications per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.24. Use HSMs for highly sensitive keys.
kry2.firstStep: Define processes for key generation, storage, distribution, rotation, and destruction for automotive encryption.
kry2.title: Key management for automotive encryption

lief1.description: Define binding information security requirements for all automotive suppliers per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.19. Require TISAX certification for suppliers handling sensitive data.
lief1.firstStep: Create a supplier requirements checklist for information security including TISAX requirements for critical suppliers.
lief1.title: Information security requirements for automotive suppliers

lief2.description: Continuously monitor the information security of your automotive suppliers through regular audits and assessments per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.22.
lief2.firstStep: Schedule annual information security audits for all critical suppliers with access to prototypes or sensitive automotive data.
lief2.title: Conduct supplier monitoring and audits

org1.description: Develop an automotive-specific information security policy and implement an ISMS per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.1. The policy must cover prototype protection and supply chain requirements.
org1.firstStep: Draft a written information security policy referencing VDA ISA requirements and have it approved by senior management.
org1.title: Establish an information security policy and ISMS

org2.description: Define clear roles and responsibilities for information security per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.2. Appoint an Information Security Officer (ISO) with direct access to senior management.
org2.firstStep: Formally appoint an Information Security Officer (ISO) and document their tasks, authority, and reporting lines.
org2.title: Define information security roles and responsibilities

per1.description: Implement pre-employment security screening processes, particularly for positions with access to prototypes or sensitive automotive data per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.6.1.
per1.firstStep: Define security screening criteria based on the sensitivity of the position (e.g., prototype access, development data).
per1.title: Conduct employee security screening

per2.description: Conduct regular automotive-specific security awareness training per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.6.3. Topics: prototype protection, supply chain risks, social engineering.
per2.firstStep: Develop a training program with automotive focus areas (prototypes, suppliers, NDA handling) for all employees.
per2.title: Conduct security awareness training for the automotive context

phy1.description: Establish physical security perimeters to protect critical areas (e.g., prototype workshops, development labs) per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.7.1. Implement access controls and visitor management.
phy1.firstStep: Identify all areas containing prototypes or highly sensitive automotive data and define security zones.
phy1.title: Set up physical security perimeters for prototypes

phy2.description: Install surveillance systems for critical areas (prototype zones, test grounds) per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.7.4. Observe data protection requirements (GDPR).
phy2.firstStep: Conduct a risk analysis for critical areas and identify zones requiring surveillance (prototypes, test grounds).
phy2.title: Implement video surveillance and physical monitoring

proto1.description: Implement specific physical protection measures for prototype vehicles and components per VDA ISA 6 (Prototype Protection module) This includes secure storage, transportation, labeling, and disposal.
proto1.firstStep: Create a prototype protection policy with clear guidelines for storage, labeling, transportation, and destruction.
proto1.title: Implement physical prototype protection

proto2.description: Classify all prototype-related information (CAD, test data, specifications) by sensitivity per VDA ISA 6 (Prototype Protection module) and implement appropriate protective measures (encryption, DRM).
proto2.firstStep: Conduct a data classification for all prototype information (public, internal, confidential, strictly confidential).
proto2.title: Classify and protect prototype information

tech1.description: Implement comprehensive asset management for all automotive-relevant assets (hardware, software, data, prototypes) with classification per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.9.
tech1.firstStep: Create a complete inventory of all automotive-related assets and classify them by protection level (e.g., prototype level).
tech1.title: Asset management and classification for automotive data

tech2.description: Implement comprehensive endpoint security measures for developer workstations and mobile devices with access to automotive data per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.1.
tech2.firstStep: Deploy endpoint protection solutions (anti-malware, EDR) on all devices with access to development data or prototypes.
tech2.title: Endpoint security for development environments

zk1.description: Implement a comprehensive access control policy for all automotive systems (development, production, prototypes) per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.5.15. Apply least-privilege and need-to-know principles.
zk1.firstStep: Document an access control policy with rules for automotive-specific systems (CAD, PLM, test databases).
zk1.title: Access control policy for automotive environments

zk2.description: Implement Privileged Access Management (PAM) for critical automotive systems (development environments, prototype networks) per VDA ISA 6 and ISO 27001 A.8.2.
zk2.firstStep: Identify all privileged accounts in automotive-critical systems and implement a PAM solution with session recording.
zk2.title: Privileged Access Management (PAM) for critical systems

cra.name: CRA
cra.description: Cybersecurity for products with digital elements

dokumentation.description: Creation and maintenance of technical documentation per Annex VII CRA
dokumentation.name: Technical Documentation
dokumentation.empoweringIntro: Evidence of conformity: complete technical documentation is not only mandatory, it is also your shield during market surveillance checks and customer enquiries.

konformitaet.description: Conformity assessment procedures and CE marking per CRA
konformitaet.name: Conformity Assessment
konformitaet.empoweringIntro: CE marking as market access: the right conformity assessment procedure secures your access to the European market and documents compliance with all CRA requirements.

sbom.description: Creation and maintenance of software composition records
sbom.name: Software Bill of Materials
sbom.empoweringIntro: Create transparency: a software bill of materials is your compass in the jungle of dependencies — it shows which components are in your product and where risks lurk.

schwachstellenmanagement.description: Systematic identification and remediation of security vulnerabilities in products with digital elements
schwachstellenmanagement.name: Vulnerability Management
schwachstellenmanagement.empoweringIntro: Vulnerabilities under control: a systematic process for detecting and remediating security flaws protects your customers and your reputation as a manufacturer.

securityByDesign.description: Integrating security into the product development lifecycle
securityByDesign.name: Security by Design
securityByDesign.empoweringIntro: Security from the start: products designed for cybersecurity from the outset have significantly fewer vulnerabilities and lower remediation costs.

supportLifecycle.description: Defining the support period for security updates
supportLifecycle.name: Support Lifecycle
supportLifecycle.empoweringIntro: Plan for the long term, build trust: a clearly communicated support period and secure supply chains strengthen your customers’ confidence in the longevity of your products.

updateManagement.description: Provision of security updates throughout the product lifecycle
updateManagement.name: Update Management
updateManagement.empoweringIntro: Protection across the entire lifecycle: secure and reliable update mechanisms ensure that your products stay protected after delivery.

vorfallMeldung.description: Reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents (Art. 14 CRA)
vorfallMeldung.name: Incident and Vulnerability Reporting
vorfallMeldung.empoweringIntro: React fast, limit the damage: clear reporting processes shorten response times for actively exploited vulnerabilities and protect your users.

assessment.euTypeExamination: EU type examination (Module B+C) or comprehensive quality management (Module H)

procedure.euTypeExamination: EU type examination or comprehensive quality management
procedure.selfWithHen: Module A with application of harmonised standards
procedure.thirdParty: EU type examination (Module B) + conformity to type (Module C)

reasons.criticalProduct: Critical product (Annex IV) — EU type examination or comprehensive quality assurance

reasons.importantClass2: Important product Class II (Annex III) — third-party assessment required
reasons.noDigitalElements: Product without digital elements — CRA not applicable
reasons.openSourceExcluded: Non-commercial open-source software — excluded from CRA (Art. 3(47))

app.description: Security of applications, email, and databases
app.name: Applications
app.empoweringIntro: Secure your applications: web applications, email systems and databases are frequent targets — targeted hardening in line with IT-Grundschutz reduces the risks considerably.

con.description: Security concepts for cryptography, data protection, and development
con.name: Concept & Planning
con.empoweringIntro: Concepts as guard rails: documented procedures for backup, cryptography and data protection provide orientation and create commitment in day-to-day work.

der.description: Security incident detection and incident response
der.name: Detection & Response
der.empoweringIntro: Detect and respond: those who detect security incidents quickly and handle them in a structured way limit the damage and learn from incidents for the future.

ind.name: Industrial IT
ind.empoweringIntro: OT security is different: industrial control systems have particular requirements — availability comes first, but without IT security operational safety is at risk too.

inf.description: Physical security of buildings and data centers
inf.name: Infrastructure
inf.empoweringIntro: Physical protection as the basis: access control, fire protection and uninterruptible power supply protect your IT infrastructure against physical threats.

isms.name: ISMS
isms.empoweringIntro: The ISMS as a steering instrument: a management system introduced in line with BSI Standard 200-1 gives you the structure to manage information security systematically and sustainably.

net.description: Network architecture, firewalls, and VPN security
net.name: Networks & Communication
net.empoweringIntro: The network as a rampart: segmentation, firewalls and VPN form the basis for keeping attackers out and preventing lateral movement.

ops.description: IT operations security, patch management, and outsourcing
ops.name: Operations
ops.empoweringIntro: Secure operation as routine: established processes for patch management, backup and logging make IT security a natural part of your daily business.

orp.name: Organization & Personnel
orp.empoweringIntro: Organisation creates clarity: defined roles, policies and training concepts ensure that everyone involved knows what is expected of them.

sys.description: Securing servers, clients, and mobile devices
sys.name: IT Systems
sys.empoweringIntro: Harden systems, reduce the attack surface: secure configuration of servers, clients and mobile devices is one of the most effective measures against cyber attacks.

meldepflichten.title: Reporting Obligations under §32 BSIG
meldepflichten.subtitle: Three-stage reporting process for significant security incidents
meldepflichten.intro: The NIS2 Implementation Act requires affected entities to report significant security incidents to the BSI without undue delay. The reporting process comprises three stages with fixed deadlines.

stage1.title: Initial Notification (24 hours)
stage1.description: Immediate initial notification to the BSI with basic information about the incident.
stage1.content: Initial assessment: nature and severity of the incident, suspected cross-border impact, initial suspicions regarding the cause.

stage2.title: Follow-up Report (72 hours)
stage2.description: Update of the initial notification with more detailed information.
stage2.content: Updated assessment: severity and impact, indicators of compromise (IoCs), countermeasures taken and planned.

stage3.title: Final Report (1 month)
stage3.deadline: No later than one month after the initial notification
stage3.description: Comprehensive final report on the incident and measures taken.
stage3.content: Detailed description: root cause analysis, type of threat, remedial measures taken, cross-border impact, lessons learned.

criteria.title: When is a Security Incident Considered Significant?
criteria.subtitle: A security incident is considered significant under §32 para. 4 BSIG if at least one of the following criteria is met:

items.disruption: Severe operational disruption of services or financial losses for the entity
items.damage: Considerable material or immaterial damage to other natural or legal persons

dsgvoComparison.title: Comparison: NIS2 vs. GDPR Reporting Obligations
dsgvoComparison.parallel: Note: If an incident falls under both NIS2 and GDPR, both reporting channels must be used in parallel.

meldepflichten.legalBasis: Legal basis: §32 BSIG in conjunction with Art. 23 NIS2 Directive

geschaeftsleitung.title: Management Accountability under §38 BSIG
geschaeftsleitung.subtitle: Personal duties and liability risks for management
geschaeftsleitung.intro: The NIS2 Implementation Act establishes personal responsibility for management under §38 BSIG. These duties are non-delegable and encompass approval, monitoring, and training.

implement.title: Approve Risk Management Measures
implement.description: Management must approve the risk management measures required under §30 BSIG.

monitor.title: Monitor Implementation
monitor.description: Management must monitor the implementation of approved measures and can be held responsible for violations.

train.title: Regular Training
train.description: Management must regularly participate in training to acquire sufficient knowledge and skills for identifying and assessing risks.

personalLiability.title: Personal Liability
personalLiability.description: Management members are liable to the entity for damages caused by breach of their duties under §38 BSIG, according to the rules applicable to the legal form.

noWaiver.title: No Waiver Possible
noWaiver.description: A waiver of the entity's claims for damages against management is void. Settlements are only permitted if the entity is insolvent.

training.title: Training Obligation
training.description: Management must regularly participate in training. This cannot be fully delegated to third parties.

items.riskApproval: Risk management measures formally approved per §30 BSIG
items.responsibility: IT security responsibilities documented and communicated
items.budget: Adequate budget allocated for IT security

items.schedule: Annual training plan for management created

items.review: At least quarterly management reviews conducted

items.insurance: D&O insurance reviewed for NIS2 coverage

geschaeftsleitung.legalBasis: Legal basis: §38 BSIG in conjunction with Art. 20 NIS2 Directive

registrierung.title: Registration Guide under §§33-34 BSIG
registrierung.subtitle: Step-by-step guide for BSI registration
registrierung.intro: Affected entities must register with the BSI within three months of the NIS2 Implementation Act taking effect. Registration is done via the BSI portal. The deadline expired on 6 March 2026, and the BSI's grace period for late registrations ended on 31 July 2026. The obligation to register remains in force regardless — entities not yet registered should do so without delay.

deadline.title: Deadlines
deadline.effective: NIS2 Implementation Act in force since: 6 December 2025 (BGBl. 2025 I No. 301)
deadline.registration: Registration deadline expired — statutory deadline 6 March 2026, BSI grace period ended 31 July 2026
deadline.note: The registration obligation applies from the time the entity first falls under the regulations.

step1.title: 1. Check Affected Status
step1.description: Use the affected check to determine whether your company falls under NIS2 and which category it is assigned to.

step2.title: 2. Create Business Account
step2.description: Create a business account on the federal Mein Unternehmenskonto (MUK) portal if you haven't already.

step3.title: 3. Access BSI Portal
step3.description: Navigate to the BSI registration portal and sign in with your business account.

step4.title: 4. Enter Details
step4.description: Enter all required data about your company (see checklist below).

step5.title: 5. Submit Registration
step5.description: Review all entries and submit the registration.

step6.title: 6. Await Confirmation
step6.description: The BSI will confirm the registration. You will receive access credentials for the reporting portal.

bussgeld.title: Penalty Calculator
bussgeld.subtitle: Estimated maximum penalty risk under §65 BSIG
bussgeld.intro: The NIS2UmsG provides for substantial fines. The amount depends on how the entity is classified. A turnover-based cap only applies above a total turnover of EUR 500 million.

explanation.besondersWichtig: For essential entities the maximum fine is up to EUR 10,000,000 (Section 65(5) sentence 1 no. 1a BSIG). Only for entities with a total turnover exceeding EUR 500 million does a cap of 2% of total turnover take its place (Section 65(6) BSIG).
explanation.wichtig: For important entities the maximum fine is up to EUR 7,000,000 (Section 65(5) sentence 1 no. 1b BSIG). Only for entities with a total turnover exceeding EUR 500 million does a cap of 1.4% of total turnover take its place (Section 65(7) BSIG).

bussgeld.note: Note: The actual penalty amount is determined by the competent authority on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the severity of the violation, possible recurrence, and countermeasures taken.

dsgvoOverlap.title: GDPR Overlap Analysis
dsgvoOverlap.subtitle: Leveraging synergies between NIS2 and GDPR compliance
dsgvoOverlap.intro: Approximately 60% of NIS2 requirements overlap with existing GDPR measures. Companies with existing GDPR compliance have a head start on NIS2 implementation.

riskAssessment.gap: NIS2 requires formal risk analysis per state of the art, not just 'appropriate' measures

incidentHandling.gap: NIS2: 24h deadline (vs. 72h GDPR), BSI as reporting authority (vs. DPA)

businessContinuity.gap: NIS2 requires comprehensive BCM including crisis management, not just recovery

supplyChain.gap: NIS2 requires IT security assessment of all suppliers, not just processors

securityMeasures.gap: NIS2 requires vulnerability management and secure procurement

effectiveness.gap: NIS2 requires demonstrable effectiveness testing (audits, pentests)

training.gap: NIS2 mandates management training (§38 BSIG) — not just general awareness

encryption.gap: NIS2 requires documented crypto concept with key management

accessControl.gap: NIS2 requires MFA, PAM, and regular access recertification

documentation.gap: NIS2 requires comprehensive documentation of all security measures
