items.i5: Measure success: Compare phishing click rates before/after training

angriffspfade.title: Common Attack Paths
angriffspfade.subtitle: How cybercriminals operate — and how to protect yourself
angriffspfade.intro: When you understand how attackers think and operate, you can protect your company more effectively. Here we show the most common attack vectors with concrete defense measures.

phishing.title: Phishing Attack
phishing.desc: Impersonates trusted senders to steal credentials

steps.s1: Attacker researches target (LinkedIn, website, org chart)
steps.s2: Creates convincingly real email (spoofed sender, copied logo)
steps.s3: Victim clicks link or opens attachment
steps.s5: Attacker uses stolen data for further access

phishing.defense: Email filters, Security awareness training, MFA, DMARC/SPF/DKIM

ransomware.title: Ransomware Attack
ransomware.desc: Encrypts company data and demands ransom

steps.s1: Initial access via phishing email or unpatched vulnerability
steps.s5: Encryption of all reachable systems and backups

ransomware.defense: Network segmentation, Offline backups, EDR, Patch management, Least privilege

supplyChain.title: Supply Chain Attack
supplyChain.desc: Attack via trusted suppliers or software updates

steps.s1: Attacker compromises software vendor or IT service provider
steps.s2: Malicious code embedded in regular software update
steps.s3: Update automatically distributed to all customers
steps.s4: Backdoor enables access to customer networks

supplyChain.defense: Supplier assessment, Software Composition Analysis, Network monitoring, Zero Trust

insider.title: Insider Threat
insider.desc: Threat from current or former employees with access rights

steps.s1: Employee with elevated access (admin, developer, executive)
steps.s3: Data exfiltration via USB, cloud, email or screenshot
steps.s4: Sabotage: Deletion of data or configuration changes
steps.s5: Detection only after weeks or months

insider.defense: Least privilege principle, Offboarding process, DLP, Logging, Four-eyes principle

bruteForce.title: Brute Force & Credential Stuffing

steps.s1: Attacker obtains leaked credentials (darknet, data breaches)
steps.s2: Automated tools test combinations against login pages
steps.s3: Password reuse leads to successful logins
steps.s4: Attacker gains access to email, VPN or cloud services

bruteForce.defense: MFA, Account lockout, Strong passwords, Credential monitoring, Rate limiting

killchain.title: Cyber Kill Chain
killchain.desc: Every attack follows a pattern. The earlier you detect it, the less damage occurs.

p1.title: Reconnaissance
p1.desc: Attacker gathers information about the target

p2.title: Weaponization
p2.desc: Malicious code is created or adapted

items.i1: Defense in Depth: Multiple defense layers instead of a single measure
items.i2: Zero Trust: Trust no one, verify everything — even within the internal network
items.i3: Patch fast: 60% of successful attacks exploit known, unpatched vulnerabilities
items.i4: MFA everywhere: Prevents 99.9% of all account-based attacks according to Microsoft
items.i5: Train, train, train: Humans remain the most important security factor

bedrohungen.title: Current Threat Landscape
bedrohungen.subtitle: The most important cyber threats for German companies — based on BSI situation report
bedrohungen.intro: The threat level in cyberspace has never been higher. Here you'll find an overview of current dangers, trends and what this specifically means for your company.

t1.title: Ransomware
t1.desc: Still the #1 threat for businesses. Double extortion (encryption + data theft) is standard.
t1.impact: Business disruption, Data loss, Ransom, Reputation damage

t2.title: Phishing & Spear Phishing
t2.desc: Increasingly sophisticated through AI-generated text. CEO fraud and business email compromise (BEC) are rising.
t2.impact: Identity theft, Financial losses, Data breaches
t2.trend: Rising — AI makes attacks more personal and convincing

t3.title: Supply Chain Attacks
t3.desc: Attacks via suppliers and IT service providers. One compromised provider affects hundreds of customers.
t3.impact: Broad damage impact, Hard to detect, Loss of trust
t3.trend: Strongly rising — increasing digitalization of supply chains

t4.title: DDoS Attacks
t4.desc: Flooding services with requests to disrupt availability. Often politically motivated or as a diversion.
t4.trend: Stable — but attacks are getting larger and more complex

t5.title: Software Vulnerabilities
t5.desc: Zero-days and known vulnerabilities in widely used software. Log4Shell and MOVEit showed the scale.
t5.impact: Unauthorized access, Data leak, System compromise
t5.trend: Permanently high — increasing software landscape complexity

t6.title: Insider Threats
t6.desc: Deliberate or accidental damage by own employees. Remote work increases the risk.
t6.impact: Data leakage, Sabotage, Hard to prove
t6.trend: Rising — Remote work and skills shortage increase risk

i1.desc: Annual damage from cyberattacks in Germany (Bitkom)

i2.desc: Of German companies have already been affected by cyberattacks

i3.desc: Vulnerabilities discovered daily on average (BSI 2024)

i4.desc: Average time until an attack is detected (IBM)

items.i1: Lower IT budgets = fewer protective measures
items.i2: No dedicated security team (often 'IT does everything')
items.i3: Valuable data: Customer data, design plans, patents
items.i4: Gateway to larger companies (supply chain attack)
items.i5: Lower resilience — one attack can be existentially threatening

items.i1: Take inventory: What systems, data and access points exist?
items.i2: Enable MFA for all accounts — now, not 'next week'
items.i3: Check your backup strategy: Does the restore actually work?
items.i4: Train your employees: People are both the strongest AND weakest defense
items.i5: Patch promptly: Automatic updates where possible, everything else within 72h

dsfa.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
dsfa.subtitle: When a DPIA is required and how to conduct one step by step
dsfa.intro: The DPIA under Art. 35 GDPR is mandatory for processing with high risk to data subjects. Neglecting it risks fines of up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 83(4) GDPR). Here is everything you need to know.

when.title: When is a DPIA required?
when.desc: A DPIA is mandatory when processing is likely to result in high risk:

items.i1: Systematic evaluation of personal aspects (profiling, scoring)
items.i2: Large-scale processing of special categories (health, biometrics)
items.i3: Systematic video surveillance of public areas
items.i4: Use of new technologies (AI, IoT, Big Data)
items.i5: Automated decisions with legal effect
items.i6: Processing data of vulnerable groups (children, employees)

s1.title: Processing Description
s1.desc: Document purpose, nature, scope, context and purposes of processing

s2.title: Necessity & Proportionality
s2.desc: Is processing necessary for the purpose? Are there less intrusive means?

s3.title: Identify Risks
s3.desc: What dangers exist for rights and freedoms of data subjects?

s4.title: Assess Risks
s4.desc: Likelihood and severity for each identified risk

s5.title: Define Measures
s5.desc: Technical and organizational measures for risk mitigation

s6.title: Evaluate Residual Risk
s6.desc: Is remaining risk acceptable? If not: consult supervisory authority

s7.title: Documentation & Review
s7.desc: Document DPIA, review regularly, update when changes occur

blacklist.title: Must-Do DPIA List
blacklist.desc: The Data Protection Conference defined processing that always requires a DPIA:

items.i1: Scoring by credit agencies or financial service providers
items.i2: Operation of rating portals
items.i3: GPS tracking of employees or vehicles
items.i4: Use of big data analysis for customer profiles
items.i5: Whistle-blowing systems
items.i6: Use of AI for recruitment

items.i1: Maintain a DPIA register — keep an overview of all assessments
items.i2: Involve the DPO early, not just at the end
items.i3: Use the BfDI PIA tool or CNIL tool as a template
items.i4: A DPIA is a living document — update regularly
items.i5: Also document the decision NOT to conduct a DPIA

vvt.title: Record of Processing Activities (RoPA)
vvt.subtitle: The mandatory GDPR document — create it step by step
vvt.intro: The RoPA under Art. 30 GDPR is mandatory for almost every company. It's the foundation of your data protection management and is the first thing requested during audits.

items.i1: All companies with more than 250 employees — always
items.i2: Companies under 250 employees, if: regular processing of personal data
items.i3: Processing of special categories (health, religion, trade union)
items.i4: Processing with risk to rights and freedoms of data subjects
items.i5: In practice: EVERY company needs a RoPA

i1.title: Name and Contact Details
i1.desc: Of the controller, representative if applicable, and DPO

i2.title: Purpose of Processing
i2.desc: Why is data processed? (e.g. payroll, marketing)

i3.title: Categories of Data Subjects
i3.desc: Customers, employees, suppliers, applicants etc.

i4.title: Categories of Personal Data
i4.desc: Name, address, email, bank details, health data etc.

i5.title: Recipient Categories
i5.desc: Who receives data? (Tax office, accountant, cloud provider)

i6.title: Third Country Transfers
i6.desc: Transfer to countries outside EU/EEA (e.g. USA)

i7.title: Deletion Deadlines
i7.desc: When is data deleted? (statutory retention periods)

items.i1: Payroll processing
items.i2: Customer management / CRM
items.i3: Email communication
items.i4: Website operation (cookies, analytics)
items.i5: Applicant management
items.i6: Video surveillance

items.i1: Start with obvious processing (payroll, CRM, email)
items.i2: Ask every department — IT often doesn't know all processing activities
items.i3: Use an Excel spreadsheet or specialized software
items.i4: Update with every new software or process change
items.i5: The RoPA is not a one-time project — it lives and grows with your company

avv.title: Data Processing Agreement (DPA)
avv.subtitle: When you need a DPA and what it must contain
avv.intro: When you have service providers process personal data (cloud, IT support, hosting), you need a DPA under Art. 28 GDPR. Without a DPA, you risk fines.

when.title: When do you need a DPA?

items.i1: Cloud services (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, AWS, Azure)
items.i2: Hosting providers (web hosting, email hosting)
items.i3: IT service providers with remote access to your systems
items.i4: Payroll accountant / tax advisor (if processing data on your behalf)
items.i5: Newsletter services (Mailchimp, CleverReach)
items.i6: Document destruction & disposal companies

i1.title: Subject and Duration
i1.desc: What is processed? How long does the contract run?

i2.title: Nature and Purpose
i2.desc: Hosting, analysis, support — clearly define the purpose

i3.title: Type of Data
i3.desc: Which data categories are processed?

i4.title: Data Subject Categories
i4.desc: Customers, employees, website visitors?

i5.title: Instruction Binding
i5.desc: The processor acts only on your instructions

i6.title: Confidentiality
i6.desc: Processor employees must be bound to confidentiality

i7.title: TOM
i7.desc: Technical and organizational measures of the processor

i8.title: Sub-processors
i8.desc: List of all sub-processors, approval requirement

i9.title: Audit Rights
i9.desc: You must be able to verify compliance

i10.title: Deletion/Return
i10.desc: What happens to data at contract end?

items.i1: Tax advisors (independently responsible, not instruction-bound)
items.i2: Lawyers (independently responsible, professional secrecy)
items.i3: Banks (payment processing in their own area of responsibility)
items.i4: Postal/parcel services (transport, not processing)

items.i1: Large providers (Microsoft, Google) have standard DPAs — review and accept
items.i2: Maintain a DPA list: Who processes what for you?
items.i3: Audit right = you MUST audit, not just can (at minimum a questionnaire)
items.i4: Without a DPA, YOU are responsible — not the service provider
items.i5: Update when changing providers or scope changes

cyberVersicherung.title: Cyber Insurance
cyberVersicherung.subtitle: Does your company need cyber insurance? Costs, coverage and exclusions
cyberVersicherung.intro: Cyber insurance can be vital in an emergency. But it doesn't replace IT security — it complements it. Here's what matters.

items.i1: Average damage per cyberattack for SMEs: EUR 95,000
items.i2: 30% of affected SMEs cannot operate normally after an attack
items.i3: GDPR fines, notification costs and forensic analyses are expensive
items.i4: Business interruptions can last weeks
items.i5: Customers and partners increasingly expect protection

i1.title: First-party Damage
i1.desc: Business interruption, data recovery, IT forensics

i2.title: Third-party Damage
i2.desc: Claims from third parties (customers, partners)

i3.title: Crisis Communication
i3.desc: PR consulting, notification of affected parties

i4.title: Legal Protection
i4.desc: Legal costs in GDPR proceedings

i5.title: Ransom
i5.desc: Coverage of ransomware payments (controversial, often capped)

items.i1: Intentional actions
items.i2: Known, unpatched vulnerabilities
items.i3: Missing basic security measures (no backup, no MFA)
items.i4: War and state-sponsored cyberattacks
items.i5: Damage from missing updates older than 30 days

prerequisites.title: Prerequisites for Coverage
prerequisites.desc: Insurers increasingly require minimum security standards:

items.i1: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) for external access
items.i2: Regular, tested backups (3-2-1 rule)
items.i3: Current patch management
items.i4: Employee training (at least annually)
items.i5: Network segmentation
items.i6: Incident response plan

items.i1: Insurance COMPLEMENTS IT security — it doesn't REPLACE it
items.i2: Compare at least 3 offers — coverage varies significantly
items.i3: Watch for sublimits (caps for individual damage types)
items.i4: Check obligations carefully — violations mean no coverage
items.i5: The better your IT security, the cheaper the premium

kostenrechner.title: IT Security Cost Calculator
kostenrechner.subtitle: What does IT security cost for your company? Reference values by company size
kostenrechner.intro: The most common question: What does IT security cost? The answer: Significantly less than a cyberattack. Here you'll find realistic cost frameworks and prioritization help.

s1.title: Solo Self-employed & Freelancers
s1.includes: Password manager, backup solution, antivirus, VPN if needed, basic training

s2.title: Micro Enterprises (1-10 employees)
s2.includes: Firewall, endpoint protection, backup, MFA, basic training, external DPO if needed

s3.title: Small Enterprises (10-50 employees)
s3.includes: Managed firewall, EDR, patch management, awareness training, external CISO, SIEM-light

s4.title: Medium Enterprises (50-250 employees)
s4.includes: SOC/MDR, SIEM, vulnerability management, CISO (internal), pentests, certification

i1.desc: Firewall, endpoint, backup, encryption, MFA

i2.desc: Awareness training, CISO, specialists, certifications

i3.desc: Policies, ISMS setup, audits, compliance

i4.desc: Pentests, consulting, managed security, forensics

i5.desc: Cyber insurance, legal protection

roi.title: Return on Security Investment
roi.conclusion: Bottom line: An investment of EUR 10,000/year in IT security can prevent damages of EUR 100,000+.

i1.title: Immediately (free/cheap)
i1.desc: Enable MFA, change passwords, install updates, check backup

i2.title: Short-term (under EUR 2,000)
i2.desc: Password manager, basic training, firewall check, antivirus

i3.title: Medium-term (EUR 2,000-10,000)
i3.desc: Awareness program, patch management, network segmentation, RoPA

i4.title: Long-term (EUR 10,000+)
i4.desc: ISMS setup, pentest, certification, SOC/SIEM, cyber insurance

items.i1: Use funding: BAFA consulting subsidy (applications until 31 Dec 2026), Mittelstand-Digital centres (free of charge)
items.i2: Open source tools: KeePass, pfSense, Wazuh, ClamAV — professional and free
items.i3: BSI Grundschutz instead of expensive consulting: Freely available, well documented
items.i4: Internal training: Videos, quizzes, micro-learning instead of expensive in-person training
items.i5: Use synergies: ISMS covers NIS2, ISO 27001 and TISAX simultaneously

scoreBadge.title: Share Your IT Security Score
scoreBadge.subtitle: Show customers and partners your IT security standard
scoreBadge.intro: A visible IT security score builds trust with customers, partners and suppliers. Learn how to use and communicate your score effectively.

items.i1: Build trust with business partners — especially in supply chains
items.i2: Competitive advantage: Customers prefer provably secure partners
items.i3: Demonstrate compliance without expensive certification
items.i4: Lower insurance premiums through documented security
items.i5: Motivate employees through visible progress

basic.title: Basic (0-40%)
basic.desc: Fundamental measures still missing. Urgent action needed.

developing.title: Developing (41-60%)
developing.desc: Initial measures implemented. Important gaps remain.

established.title: Established (61-80%)
established.desc: Solid foundation. Optimization potential in details.

i1.title: Website Badge
i1.desc: Embed on your website as a trust seal

i2.title: Email Signature
i2.desc: Link score badge in your email signature

i3.title: Proposal Documents
i3.desc: Demonstrate IT security standard in tenders

i4.title: Supplier Questionnaires
i4.desc: Use score as evidence in customer questionnaires

items.i1: Complete the full assessment first for a meaningful score
items.i2: Update your score regularly — at least quarterly
items.i3: A score is not a certificate — communicate honestly
items.i4: Use the score internally as a motivation tool for your team

lieferantenAmpel.title: Supplier Security Assessment
lieferantenAmpel.subtitle: Check and document IT security in your supply chain
lieferantenAmpel.intro: NIS2 and ISO 27001 require the assessment of suppliers and service providers. Here you'll learn how to systematically check IT security in your supply chain.

items.i1: NIS2 Section 30(2) No. 4: Supply chain security is mandatory
items.i2: 60% of cyberattacks come through the supply chain (Gartner)
items.i3: One compromised service provider endangers all customers
items.i4: Insurers increasingly require supplier assessment
items.i5: Customers actively ask about your supply chain security

i1.title: Certifications
i1.desc: ISO 27001, SOC 2, TISAX, BSI IT-Grundschutz available?

i2.title: Data Protection
i2.desc: DPA in place, GDPR-compliant, DPO appointed?

i3.title: Patch Management
i3.desc: Regular updates, SLA for critical patches?

i4.title: Access Control
i4.desc: MFA, Least Privilege, regular access reviews?

i5.title: Incident Response
i5.desc: Emergency plan in place, notification obligation to you agreed?

i8.title: Sub-contractors
i8.desc: Control over supplier's own supply chain?

green.title: Green — Uncritical
green.desc: All essential criteria met. Cooperation without restrictions.

yellow.title: Yellow — Conditional
yellow.desc: Partially met. Cooperation with conditions and action plan.

red.title: Red — Critical
red.desc: Essential criteria not met. Cooperation only under strict conditions or rejection.

items.i1: Create a standardized questionnaire for all suppliers
items.i2: Prioritize: Assess critical suppliers (IT, cloud, data) first
items.i3: Contractually agree on incident notification obligations
items.i4: Conduct assessment at least annually, semi-annually for critical suppliers
items.i5: Document EVERYTHING — auditors will ask for evidence

jahresbericht.title: IT Security Annual Report
jahresbericht.subtitle: Annual reporting for management and oversight
jahresbericht.intro: An annual IT security report is best practice and effectively mandatory for NIS2-regulated companies. Here you'll learn what belongs in it and how to structure it.

items.i1: NIS2: Management must actively oversee IT security
items.i2: ISO 27001: Management review is a mandatory component
items.i3: Liability protection: Documented duty of care by management
items.i4: Budget planning: Evidence-based argumentation for IT security budget
items.i5: Measure progress: Year-over-year comparison shows development

s1.title: Executive Summary
s1.desc: Key statements for management on one page

s2.title: Maturity Level & Score
s2.desc: Current status, comparison to previous year, target values

s3.title: Incidents & Reports
s3.desc: Number, type and handling of security incidents

s4.title: Implemented Measures
s4.desc: What was implemented during the reporting period?

s5.title: Open Risks
s5.desc: Known risks with assessment and action plan

s6.title: Training & Awareness
s6.desc: Conducted training, participation rate, phishing test results

s8.title: Budget & Resources
s8.desc: Expenditure, comparison to plan, budget request for next year

s9.title: Outlook & Recommendations
s9.desc: Planned measures, threat trends, strategic recommendations

items.i1: Maximum 15-20 pages — management won't read 100-page documents
items.i2: Visualize: Traffic lights, trend arrows, charts instead of tables
items.i3: Translate risks into money — 'Ransomware risk: EUR 200,000' is stronger than 'high risk'
items.i4: Show year-over-year comparison — progress motivates
items.i5: Concrete action recommendations with budget and timeline

digitalerNachlass.title: Digital Estate & Emergency Access
digitalerNachlass.subtitle: What happens to your IT systems if you become unavailable?
digitalerNachlass.intro: What happens when the IT manager or CEO suddenly becomes unavailable? Without emergency access, the company stops. Here's how to prepare.

items.i1: CEO passes away — no one knows the admin password
items.i2: IT manager has an accident — only they know the server credentials
items.i3: Freelancer becomes seriously ill — hosting and domain expire
items.i4: Employee is terminated — takes knowledge of configurations with them

i1.title: Master Password Envelope
i1.desc: Password manager master password in sealed envelope, in safe or with notary

i2.title: Access Documentation
i2.desc: List of all critical systems with access information (stored encrypted)

i3.title: Trusted Person
i3.desc: At least 2 people who can gain access in emergencies

i4.title: Domain Registrar
i4.desc: Store login credentials for domain provider

i5.title: Hosting Access
i5.desc: Server/hosting access for at least 2 people

i6.title: Email Admin
i6.desc: Admin access to email infrastructure (Exchange, Google Workspace)

i7.title: Banking
i7.desc: Powers of attorney and access for online banking

i8.title: Contracts & Licenses
i8.desc: Overview of all IT contracts, notice periods, contacts

i9.title: Backup Access
i9.desc: Where are backups? How to access them? Encryption passwords?

i10.title: Testamentary Provisions
i10.desc: Regulate digital estate in will (especially for sole proprietors)

items.i1: The 'bus factor' principle: No critical knowledge should reside with only one person
items.i2: Update password envelopes regularly (at least semi-annually)
items.i3: Test emergency access: Can Person B actually reach everything?
items.i4: For freelancers: Deposit a digital legacy document with a notary
items.i5: Four-eyes principle: No single person should have unrestricted access

cloudCheck.title: Cloud Security Check
cloudCheck.subtitle: Check the IT security of your cloud services — systematically and traceably
cloudCheck.intro: Cloud services are convenient but not automatically secure. From Microsoft 365 to AWS to small SaaS tools — every cloud service needs a security assessment.

i1.title: Loss of Control
i1.desc: Data resides on third-party servers — you must trust the provider

i2.title: Data Protection
i2.desc: Many cloud providers are US-based — third-country transfer issues

i3.title: Vendor Lock-in
i3.desc: Dependency on one provider — data migration can be difficult

i4.title: Shared Responsibility
i4.desc: Security is shared — provider secures infrastructure, YOU secure your data

i5.title: Shadow IT
i5.desc: Employees use cloud services without IT department knowledge

i6.title: Misconfiguration
i6.desc: Open S3 buckets, wrong permissions — #1 cause of cloud data leaks

items.i1: MFA enabled for all cloud accounts
items.i2: Admin accounts separate and specially protected
items.i3: Regular access rights review (at least quarterly)
items.i4: Immediate deactivation on employee departure
items.i5: SSO (Single Sign-On) used where possible

items.i1: DPA signed with every cloud provider
items.i2: Server location known (EU preferred)
items.i3: Encryption in transit and at rest enabled
items.i4: Backup strategy for cloud data defined
items.i5: Data deletion process agreed for contract end

items.i1: Default security settings hardened (not left as default)
items.i2: Logging and monitoring enabled
items.i3: Network access restricted (IP whitelisting where possible)
items.i4: Automatic updates/patches enabled at provider
items.i5: Regular configuration reviews scheduled

saas.title: SaaS
saas.responsibility: Provider: Almost everything. You: Access + Data

paas.title: PaaS
paas.desc: Platform as a Service (Azure App Service, Heroku)
paas.responsibility: Provider: Infrastructure + Runtime. You: Application + Data

iaas.title: IaaS
iaas.desc: Infrastructure as a Service (AWS EC2, Azure VMs)
iaas.responsibility: Provider: Hardware + Network. You: OS + Application + Data

items.i1: Maintain a cloud inventory: What services do you actually use?
items.i2: Evaluate every new cloud service BEFORE it's introduced
items.i3: Prefer EU providers or providers with EU data centers
items.i4: Test the data export function — can you get your data back?
items.i5: Train employees on shadow IT risks

benchmark.title: IT Security Benchmark
benchmark.subtitle: Where does your company stand? Industry averages and reference values
benchmark.intro: How good is your IT security really? Compare yourself with industry averages and best practice values to identify strengths and weaknesses.

averages.title: Industry Averages IT Security
averages.desc: Based on BSI situation report, Bitkom studies and industry reports:

i1.desc: Heavily regulated (DORA, BaFin), high standards

i2.desc: KRITIS-regulated, but often underfunded

i3.desc: OT security often neglected, TISAX drives improvement

i4.desc: PCI DSS for card payments, otherwise heterogeneous

i5.desc: Self-interest + customer requirements drive standards

selfAssess.title: Quick Self-Assessment

items.i1: Do ALL employees have MFA enabled?
items.i2: Was a backup restore tested in the last 12 months?
items.i3: Is there a written IT security policy?
items.i4: Were all employees trained in the last 12 months?
items.i5: Does a documented emergency plan exist?

selfAssess.scoring: 0-1 Yes: Immediate action needed | 2-3 Yes: On the way | 4-5 Yes: Good foundation

items.i1: Don't compare with corporations — orient yourself to similarly sized companies
items.i2: Focus on KPIs with the greatest leverage: MFA, backup, training
items.i3: Measure quarterly and document progress
items.i4: Use IT-Sicherheitskompass as a benchmark tool for all regulations
items.i5: Share results with management — numbers make an impact

poster.title: IT Security Posters & Notices
poster.subtitle: Printable security rules for office, server room and break area
poster.intro: Simple, clearly visible rules work. Hang these posters and remind your team daily of the most important IT security rules.

rules.r3: Don't open suspicious emails — report them!
rules.r5: Never plug in unknown USB drives
rules.r6: Install updates immediately — not 'Remind me later'
rules.r9: Report security incidents immediately — never cover up
rules.r10: Clean desk: Lock away documents, clear the printer

rules.r1: Urgent request: 'Act now!' / 'Your account will be locked!'
rules.r2: Unknown sender or slightly altered domain (rnicrosoft.com)
rules.r4: Link leads somewhere different than displayed (hover to check!)

rules.r3: A unique password for EVERY service
rules.r5: Never on sticky notes on the monitor, never share via email

rules.r2: Disconnect device from network (pull cable / turn off WiFi)
rules.r4: DON'T delete or change anything (evidence preservation)
rules.r5: Document the incident (What? When? How noticed?)

items.i1: Hang posters at eye level next to printer, coffee machine and entrance area
items.i2: Change posters every 3 months — familiarity reduces effectiveness
items.i3: Use posters as conversation starters in team meetings
items.i4: Print on A3 for best readability

radar.title: Threat Radar
radar.subtitle: Current cyber threats at a glance — what you need to watch out for now
radar.intro: The threat landscape changes constantly. This radar shows you the currently most relevant threats for German SMEs with concrete recommendations.

i1.title: Ransomware Groups (LockBit, BlackCat, Cl0p)
i1.desc: Actively targeting German SMEs, double extortion standard

i2.title: AI-powered Phishing
i2.desc: Perfect language, personalized, almost undetectable

i3.title: Unpatched Exchange Servers
i3.desc: Still the #1 entry point for on-premise systems

i1.title: Supply Chain Attacks via SaaS
i1.desc: Compromise through cloud service providers increasing

i2.title: QR Code Phishing (Quishing)
i2.desc: Fake QR codes in emails and physically

i3.title: MFA Fatigue Attacks
i3.desc: Attackers bombard with MFA requests until victim accepts

i1.title: AI-generated Deepfakes
i1.desc: CEO fraud via video/audio becoming more realistic

i2.title: IoT Botnets
i2.desc: Smart devices in corporate network as entry points

i3.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
i3.desc: Prepare encryption today for quantum computers tomorrow

i1.title: Social Engineering
i1.desc: Humans remain the primary target — training is mandatory

i2.title: Insider Threats
i2.desc: Remote work increases risk of uncontrolled data access

i3.title: Legacy Software Vulnerabilities
i3.desc: Old systems without updates are ticking time bombs

items.i1: Upgrade MFA with phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2/Passkeys)
items.i2: Strengthen email security: Configure DMARC, SPF, DKIM
items.i3: Verify offline backups — does the restore actually work?
items.i4: Train employees on AI phishing and quishing
items.i5: Check external attack surface: What's reachable from outside?

beraterModus.title: IT Security Consultant Guide
beraterModus.subtitle: Use IT-Sicherheitskompass professionally for your clients
beraterModus.intro: Are you an IT consultant, CISO or freelancer wanting to use IT-Sicherheitskompass for your clients? Here's how to professionally integrate the tool into your consulting process.

s1.title: Initial Meeting & Navigator
s1.desc: Walk through the Navigator with the client to identify relevant regulations

s2.title: Quick Check per Regulation
s2.desc: Use the quick check as an entry point — gives the client immediate understanding

s3.title: Gap Analysis (Assessment)
s3.desc: Conduct the full assessment — ideally in a workshop with the client

s4.title: Present Results
s4.desc: Use the Executive Summary button for management and Excel export for details

s5.title: Derive Action Plan
s5.desc: Prioritize quick wins and create a realistic roadmap

s6.title: Accompany Implementation
s6.desc: Use the progress tracker to document implementation

s7.title: Review & Report
s7.desc: Quarterly reviews, create annual report, document score development

items.i1: Free and immediately available — no license budget needed
items.i2: 15 regulations & standards in one platform — no tool chaos
items.i3: Concrete action recommendations instead of abstract theory
items.i4: Progress measurement: Improvements are visible and provable
items.i5: No registration, no data in the cloud — everything local in the browser

i1.title: Initial Analysis (1 day)
i1.desc: Navigator + quick check + results presentation

i2.title: Full Assessment (2-3 days)
i2.desc: Gap analysis + action plan + management report

i3.title: Monthly Accompaniment
i3.desc: Implementation support, quarterly reviews, training

items.i1: Never conduct the assessment alone — involve the client
items.i2: Always start with quick wins — visible successes build trust

items.i4: Document progress visually — executives love charts

hub.title: IT Security by Industry
hub.subtitle: Which regulations, risks, and measures are relevant for your industry? Find industry-specific guidance.
hub.intro: Every industry has its own IT security requirements. Whether legal obligations like NIS2 and GDPR or industry-specific standards like TISAX or PCI DSS — here you'll find a compact overview for your sector.

logistik.title: IT Security for Transport & Logistics
logistik.subtitle: Protect supply chains, meet NIS2 obligations, secure operations
logistik.metaDesc: IT security for freight forwarders, logistics companies, and transport providers. NIS2, GDPR, KRITIS — all requirements at a glance.
logistik.intro: The transport and logistics industry is increasingly digitalized — from telematics to warehouse management to route planning. At the same time, regulatory requirements through NIS2 are growing and IT dependency makes the industry vulnerable.

nis2.reason: Transport sector in NIS2 Annex I — all medium and large companies affected

dsgvo.reason: Driver data, customer data, GPS tracking — personal data in core business

kritis.reason: Large logistics companies may be classified as critical infrastructure operators

tisax.reason: Automotive suppliers in logistics need TISAX conformity

iso27001.reason: Major clients increasingly require ISO 27001 certification

items.i1: Ransomware paralyzes route planning and warehouse management — supply chain stops
items.i2: GPS spoofing and telematics manipulation endanger transport routes
items.i3: Phishing via forged freight documents and delivery notices
items.i4: Unsecured interfaces to customer systems (EDI, API)
items.i5: Driver data leaks through unsecured mobile devices
items.i6: Supply chain attacks via compromised subcontractors

i1.title: MFA for all IT systems
i1.desc: Telematics portal, TMS, WMS — enable two-factor authentication everywhere

i2.title: Backup strategy 3-2-1
i2.desc: Daily backups of route planning and customer master data, separate storage

i3.title: Network segmentation
i3.desc: Strictly separate office IT, telematics, and warehouse WiFi

i4.title: Employee training
i4.desc: Awareness for phishing via forged freight communication

i5.title: Mobile Device Management
i5.desc: Centrally manage and secure driver smartphones and tablets

i6.title: Supplier assessment
i6.desc: Include IT security requirements in subcontractor contracts

logistik.quickWin: Start with the NIS2 quick check — as a transport company, you are very likely affected.

gesundheit.title: IT Security in Healthcare
gesundheit.subtitle: Protect patient data, secure medical devices, ensure compliance
gesundheit.metaDesc: IT security for medical practices, clinics, laboratories, and healthcare providers. GDPR, NIS2, KRITIS — all obligations explained.
gesundheit.intro: Healthcare processes highly sensitive patient data and is increasingly targeted by cyberattacks. The combination of strict data protection requirements (GDPR Art. 9), NIS2 obligations, and the criticality of medical devices makes IT security a top priority.

nis2.reason: Healthcare sector in NIS2 Annex I — hospitals, laboratories, pharmaceutical companies affected

dsgvo.reason: Art. 9 GDPR — health data are special categories with enhanced protection requirements

kritis.reason: Hospitals with 30,000+ inpatient cases/year are critical infrastructure

iso27001.reason: Basis for industry-specific security standards (B3S Hospital)

items.i1: Ransomware attacks on hospitals — surgery cancellations and patient endangerment
items.i2: Patient data leaks with severe GDPR consequences (Art. 9 special categories)
items.i3: Connected medical devices (IoMT) as attack vectors
items.i4: Unencrypted communication between practices, laboratories, and insurers
items.i5: Social engineering against clinic staff with high success rate
items.i6: Outdated software on medical systems without patching options

i1.title: Encrypt all patient data
i1.desc: At-rest and in-transit — especially for transmissions to labs and insurers

i2.title: IoMT network segmentation
i2.desc: Isolate medical devices in dedicated VLANs, no direct internet access

i3.title: Role-based access control
i3.desc: Only treating physicians see patient records — principle of least privilege

i4.title: Regular privacy training
i4.desc: Mandatory training for all staff with patient contact

i5.title: Cyberattack emergency plan
i5.desc: Documented procedure for IT outage including analog fallback

i6.title: Medical device patch management
i6.desc: Coordinated with manufacturers, documented and monitored

gesundheit.quickWin: Start with the GDPR assessment — patient data requires the highest level of protection.

fertigung.title: IT Security for Manufacturing & Production
fertigung.subtitle: OT security, securing Industry 4.0, preventing production outages
fertigung.metaDesc: IT security for manufacturing companies. NIS2, CRA, TISAX — properly securing OT security and Industry 4.0.
fertigung.intro: The convergence of IT and OT (Operational Technology) in manufacturing creates new attack surfaces. Connected production systems, IoT sensors, and digital twins offer efficiency gains — but also entry points for cyberattacks.

nis2.reason: Manufacturing in NIS2 Annex II — critical product manufacturers affected

cra.reason: Cyber Resilience Act affects manufacturers of products with digital elements

tisax.reason: Automotive suppliers need TISAX for VDA business relationships

iso27001.reason: Major clients and OEMs increasingly require ISO 27001 certification

dsgvo.reason: Employee data, camera systems, access control — GDPR-relevant

items.i1: Ransomware stops production line — costs of 100,000+ EUR per day of downtime
items.i2: Outdated PLC/SCADA systems without security updates
items.i3: Unsecured OT networks with direct internet access
items.i4: Industrial espionage through compromised development computers
items.i5: Supply chain attacks via infected firmware updates
items.i6: USB-based malware distribution in the production environment

i1.title: OT/IT segmentation
i1.desc: Physically separate production network from office IT (Purdue Model)

i2.title: OT asset inventory
i2.desc: Catalog all PLCs, HMIs, SCADA systems and document firmware versions

i3.title: USB control
i3.desc: Lock USB ports in production or control via whitelist

i4.title: PLC program backup
i4.desc: Regular backup of all control programs and configurations

i5.title: Secure remote maintenance
i5.desc: VPN mandatory and MFA for all remote access to production systems

i6.title: OT incident response plan
i6.desc: Specific emergency plan for production outages due to cyberattacks

fertigung.quickWin: Start with the NIS2 quick check — most manufacturing companies fall under Annex II.

handel.title: IT Security for Retail & E-Commerce
handel.subtitle: Protect customer data, secure payment systems, harden online shops
handel.metaDesc: IT security for retail and online shops. PCI DSS, GDPR, NIS2 — all requirements for the retail sector.
handel.intro: Whether brick-and-mortar retail or e-commerce — customer data and payment information are processed everywhere. The combination of PCI DSS requirements, GDPR obligations, and growing cyber threats against online shops makes professional IT security essential.

pciDss.reason: Every merchant accepting card payments must comply with PCI DSS

dsgvo.reason: Customer data, newsletters, order history — extensive GDPR obligations

nis2.reason: Online marketplaces and large retail companies fall under NIS2

iso27001.reason: B2B customers and insurers increasingly require certifications

cra.reason: Private label electronics or IoT products are subject to the CRA

items.i1: Credit card data theft through compromised POS terminals
items.i2: Magecart attacks on online shop payment forms
items.i3: Customer data leaks through unsecured shop databases
items.i4: DDoS attacks on online shops during peak times (Black Friday, Christmas)
items.i5: Phishing against employees with access to payment systems
items.i6: Fake returns and fraud through compromised customer accounts

i1.title: PCI DSS compliance
i1.desc: Complete SAQ, process card data only through certified payment providers

i2.title: Web Application Firewall
i2.desc: Deploy WAF in front of online shop — protection against SQL injection and XSS

i3.title: Regular shop updates
i3.desc: Keep CMS, plugins, and payment modules always up to date

i4.title: Minimize customer data
i4.desc: Only collect necessary data, enforce deletion periods (GDPR Art. 5)

i5.title: DDoS protection
i5.desc: Use CDN with DDoS mitigation for the online shop

i6.title: Monitoring & alerting
i6.desc: Automatically detect and report unusual transaction patterns

handel.quickWin: Start with the PCI DSS check — if you accept card payments, it's mandatory.

itDienstleister.title: IT Security for IT Service Providers
itDienstleister.subtitle: Protect customer systems, build trust, demonstrate compliance
itDienstleister.metaDesc: IT security for IT service providers, MSPs, and system houses. ISO 27001, SOC 2, NIS2 — compliance as competitive advantage.
itDienstleister.intro: IT service providers are both multipliers and targets. A compromised MSP can endanger hundreds of clients. At the same time, certifications like ISO 27001 and SOC 2 are increasingly prerequisites for winning clients.

nis2.reason: ICT service providers fall directly under NIS2 — MSPs, cloud providers, data centers

iso27001.reason: Standard requirement from enterprise clients — competitive advantage

soc2.reason: International clients expect SOC 2 Type II reports

c5.reason: Cloud services for public sector clients require C5 attestation

dsgvo.reason: DPA obligation — IT service providers are almost always data processors

risks.title: Typical IT risks for IT service providers

items.i1: Supply chain attack via MSP — one compromised access endangers all clients
items.i2: Privileged access abuse by employees with admin rights at client sites
items.i3: Unsecured remote access to client systems
items.i4: Insufficient tenant separation in multi-tenant environments
items.i5: Outdated monitoring tools with known vulnerabilities
items.i6: Missing documentation and reporting obligations for security incidents

actions.title: Top measures for IT service providers

i1.title: Privileged Access Management
i1.desc: PAM solution for all client access — time-limited, logged, with MFA

i2.title: ISO 27001 certification
i2.desc: Build ISMS as a foundation of trust and competitive advantage

i3.title: Verify tenant separation
i3.desc: Strictly isolate network, data, and access between clients

i4.title: Client incident response
i4.desc: Documented process for security incidents at client sites

i5.title: DPA management
i5.desc: Conclude and maintain standardized DPAs with all clients

i6.title: Team security awareness
i6.desc: Your own employees are the first line of defense — train regularly

itDienstleister.quickWin: Start with the ISO 27001 assessment — the most important standard for IT service providers.

energie.title: IT Security for Energy Providers
energie.subtitle: Protect critical infrastructure, meet KRITIS obligations, ensure supply security
energie.metaDesc: IT security for energy providers and utilities. NIS2, KRITIS, BSI IT-Grundschutz — all obligations for the energy sector.
energie.intro: The energy sector is the backbone of society and thus a top target for cyberattacks. From grid operators to municipal utilities to wind farm operators — regulatory requirements are high and the consequences of outages are severe.

nis2.reason: Energy sector in NIS2 Annex I — essential entities with highest requirements

kritis.reason: Energy providers are classic critical infrastructure operators under BSI-KritisV

bsiGrundschutz.reason: BSI IT-Grundschutz is the de-facto standard for the industry

dsgvo.reason: Smart meter data and customer master data are personal data

risks.title: Typical IT risks in the energy sector

items.i1: State-sponsored attacks on energy infrastructure (APT groups)
items.i2: Compromise of SCADA/ICS systems in substations
items.i3: Ransomware against IT systems with spillover to OT networks
items.i4: Smart meter manipulation and billing fraud
items.i5: Attacks on wind farm remote control and PV inverters
items.i6: Insider threats from privileged technicians with remote access

i1.title: IT/OT segmentation per IEC 62443
i1.desc: Strict separation of office IT and control systems, DMZ in between

i2.title: Implement BSI-Grundschutz
i2.desc: Systematic ISMS buildup according to BSI Standard 200-x

i3.title: 24/7 monitoring
i3.desc: Security Operations Center (SOC) for real-time monitoring

i4.title: Set up KRITIS reporting
i4.desc: Establish reporting channels to BSI and test regularly

i5.title: Red team exercises
i5.desc: Regular attack simulations on critical systems

i6.title: Emergency exercises
i6.desc: Annual exercises for blackout scenarios with IT outage

energie.quickWin: Start with the KRITIS check — as an energy provider, you are subject to the strictest requirements.

automotive.title: IT Security for Automotive & Suppliers
automotive.subtitle: Meet TISAX requirements, protect production secrets, secure supply chain
automotive.metaDesc: IT security for automotive suppliers. TISAX, NIS2, CRA — all requirements for the automotive industry.
automotive.intro: The automotive industry places particularly high demands on information security. TISAX is the industry-specific standard required by all OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers. Additionally, NIS2 obligations and the Cyber Resilience Act apply to connected vehicle components.

tisax.reason: Mandatory standard for all VDA business relationships — OEMs and Tier-1 require TISAX

nis2.reason: Vehicle manufacturing in NIS2 Annex II — manufacturers and key suppliers affected

cra.reason: Connected vehicle components (V2X, OBD) fall under the CRA

iso27001.reason: TISAX is based on ISO 27001 — often pursued in parallel

dsgvo.reason: Connected cars generate personal data — GDPR-relevant

risks.title: Typical IT risks in the automotive industry

items.i1: Industrial espionage on development data (prototypes, CAD, BOMs)
items.i2: Ransomware in production — just-in-time supply chain collapses
items.i3: Compromised firmware in ECUs and connected vehicle components
items.i4: Supplier attacks via insecure interfaces to Tier-2/Tier-3 suppliers
items.i5: Data exfiltration through unprotected development environments
items.i6: Loss of TISAX certification due to security deficiencies — business loss

actions.title: Top measures for the automotive industry

i1.title: Prepare TISAX assessment
i1.desc: Systematically work through ISA catalog, perform gap analysis

i2.title: Prototype protection
i2.desc: Encrypt development data, strictly enforce need-to-know principle

i3.title: Supply chain security
i3.desc: Include IT security requirements in supplier contracts

i4.title: Secure development (SSDLC)
i4.desc: Security-by-design for all software components in vehicles

i5.title: Network segmentation
i5.desc: Strictly separate development, production, and administration

i6.title: Classified information handling
i6.desc: Protect prototype photos, BOMs, and CAD data according to VDA-ISA

automotive.quickWin: Start with the TISAX check — no TISAX label, no business with OEMs.

finanzen.title: IT Security for Financial Services
finanzen.subtitle: Ensure DORA compliance, protect customer data, meet regulatory obligations
finanzen.metaDesc: IT security for banks, insurers, and financial service providers. DORA, NIS2, PCI DSS — all regulations at a glance.
finanzen.intro: The financial sector is subject to the strictest IT security requirements of any industry. With DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) effective since 2025, an EU-wide regulation mandates IT risk management, incident reporting, and third-party risk management.

dora.reason: DORA has been mandatory since January 2025 — comprehensive IT resilience requirements

nis2.reason: Financial sector in NIS2 Annex I — in addition to sector-specific requirements

pciDss.reason: Card processing requires PCI DSS compliance — strictly audited

iso27001.reason: De-facto standard, often seen as minimum requirement by BaFin

dsgvo.reason: Financial data is among the most sensitive personal data

risks.title: Typical IT risks in the financial sector

items.i1: Targeted attacks on online banking and payment processing
items.i2: Insider trading through compromised analyst computers
items.i3: Third-party risks from cloud outsourcing and FinTech partners
items.i4: DDoS attacks on trading platforms and online banking
items.i5: Compliance violations due to inadequate IT security documentation
items.i6: Social engineering against employees with access to financial systems

actions.title: Top measures for financial service providers

i1.title: Build DORA compliance
i1.desc: Establish ICT Risk Management Framework, Incident Reporting, and Digital Resilience Testing

i2.title: Third-party risk management
i2.desc: Assess and monitor all IT service providers — DORA Articles 28-44

i3.title: Threat-led penetration testing
i3.desc: TLPT per DORA Article 26 — realistic attack simulations

i4.title: Business continuity management
i4.desc: Detailed recovery plans for all critical business processes

i5.title: End-to-end encryption
i5.desc: Consistently encrypt all financial transactions and customer data

i6.title: Regulatory reporting
i6.desc: Establish reporting processes to BaFin and BSI and practice regularly

finanzen.quickWin: Start with the DORA assessment — DORA has been mandatory since January 2025.

ic1.title: Build a Hardware Inventory
ic1.description: Create a complete directory of all network devices with automated detection of new devices.
ic1.firstStep: Start with a network scanning tool such as Nmap or a commercial asset discovery solution.

ic2.title: Implement a Software Allowlist
ic2.description: Define approved software and block unauthorized installations.
ic2.firstStep: Create a list of all approved applications and enable AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies.

dp1.title: Implement Data Classification
dp1.description: Introduce a classification scheme (public, internal, confidential, strictly confidential).
dp1.firstStep: Define 3-4 classification levels and train all employees on proper handling procedures.

dp2.title: Enable Encryption
dp2.description: Encrypt all sensitive data at rest and in transit.
dp2.firstStep: Enable BitLocker/FileVault on all endpoints and enforce TLS for all internal services.

sc1.title: Apply CIS Benchmarks
sc1.description: Harden all systems according to CIS Benchmark guidelines.
sc1.firstStep: Download the CIS Benchmarks for your operating systems and review the current configuration.

sc2.title: Deploy MFA Organization-wide
sc2.description: Enable multi-factor authentication for all critical systems and administrative access.
sc2.firstStep: Start with MFA for email, VPN, and cloud services — the most common attack targets.

vm1.title: Deploy a Vulnerability Scanner
vm1.description: Perform weekly vulnerability scans and prioritize patches by CVSS score.
vm1.firstStep: Set up OpenVAS or a commercial scanner and schedule weekly scans.

vm2.title: Centralized Log Collection
vm2.description: Implement a SIEM or centralized log management for all critical systems.
vm2.firstStep: Start by forwarding firewall, AD, and server logs to a central syslog server.

rn1.title: Implement 3-2-1 Backup
rn1.description: 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 offsite — with monthly recovery tests.
rn1.firstStep: Review your current backup strategy and schedule your first recovery test.

rn2.title: Network Segmentation
rn2.description: Segment your network based on protection requirements and restrict lateral movement.
rn2.firstStep: Identify your most critical systems and create a VLAN concept.

so1.title: Launch an Awareness Program
so1.description: Establish regular security awareness training with simulated phishing tests.
so1.firstStep: Choose an awareness platform and schedule the first phishing simulation.

so2.title: Create an Incident Response Plan
so2.description: Document an IR plan with roles, escalation paths, and communication templates.
so2.firstStep: Define the IR team and create a one-page emergency contact plan.

cl1.title: BCM-Politik erstellen
cl1.description: Verabschieden Sie eine BC-Politik, die Scope, Ziele und Verantwortlichkeiten definiert.
cl1.firstStep: Erstellen Sie einen einseitigen Politik-Entwurf und legen Sie ihn der Geschäftsleitung zur Freigabe vor.

cl2.title: BCM-Organisation aufbauen
cl2.description: Benennen Sie einen BC-Manager und definieren Sie Rollen für alle Notfall-Teams.
cl2.firstStep: Identifizieren Sie den BC-Verantwortlichen und erstellen Sie eine RACI-Matrix.

pl1.title: Risikoanalyse durchführen
pl1.description: Identifizieren Sie alle Bedrohungen für Ihre Geschäftskontinuität und bewerten Sie diese.
pl1.firstStep: Listen Sie die Top-10-Bedrohungen für Ihren Standort und Ihre IT-Systeme auf.

sr1.title: BC-Schulungsprogramm starten
sr1.description: Schulen Sie alle Mitarbeiter in ihren Notfall-Rollen und -Verantwortlichkeiten.
sr1.firstStep: Erstellen Sie eine kurze Notfall-Einweisung für alle neuen Mitarbeiter.

bi1.title: Business Impact Analyse erstellen
bi1.description: Bewerten Sie alle Geschäftsprozesse hinsichtlich Kritikalität und maximal tolerierbarer Ausfallzeit.
bi1.firstStep: Identifizieren Sie Ihre 5 kritischsten Geschäftsprozesse und deren Abhängigkeiten.

bi2.title: RTO/RPO definieren
bi2.description: Legen Sie Recovery Time und Recovery Point Objectives für alle kritischen Prozesse fest.
bi2.firstStep: Bestimmen Sie für jeden kritischen Prozess die maximal akzeptable Ausfallzeit.

bs1.title: BC-Pläne dokumentieren
bs1.description: Erstellen Sie konkrete Notfallpläne mit Schritt-für-Schritt-Anleitungen für jeden kritischen Prozess.
bs1.firstStep: Beginnen Sie mit dem kritischsten Prozess und erstellen Sie einen Wiederanlaufplan.

bs2.title: Übungsprogramm etablieren
bs2.description: Planen Sie mindestens jährliche BC-Übungen von Tischübungen bis Vollübungen.
bs2.firstStep: Planen Sie eine Tischübung (Tabletop) mit dem Management-Team.

bs3.title: Krisenkommunikation vorbereiten
bs3.description: Definieren Sie Eskalationswege, Kommunikationsvorlagen und Kontaktlisten.
bs3.firstStep: Erstellen Sie eine Notfall-Kontaktliste mit allen internen und externen Ansprechpartnern.

ei1.title: BCM-KPIs definieren
ei1.description: Messen Sie die Wirksamkeit Ihres BCM anhand definierter Kennzahlen.
ei1.firstStep: Definieren Sie 5 KPIs (z.B. Übungshäufigkeit, Plan-Aktualität, Wiederherstellungszeit).

ei2.title: Interne BCM-Audits planen
ei2.description: Führen Sie jährliche interne Audits des BCMS durch.
ei2.firstStep: Erstellen Sie eine Audit-Checkliste basierend auf ISO 22301 Anforderungen.

ei3.title: Lessons Learned Prozess einführen
ei3.description: Dokumentieren und implementieren Sie Verbesserungen nach jeder Übung oder jedem Vorfall.
ei3.firstStep: Erstellen Sie ein Lessons-Learned-Template für die nächste Übung.

gv1.description: Create a documented strategy that aligns cybersecurity with business objectives.
gv1.firstStep: Define the top 5 cybersecurity goals in alignment with your business strategy.

gv2.title: Establish risk governance
gv2.description: Implement regular cybersecurity risk reporting to executive management.
gv2.firstStep: Create a monthly risk dashboard for executive management.

id1.title: Build an asset inventory
id1.description: Create a comprehensive inventory of all IT assets including cloud services.
id1.firstStep: Start by inventorying all cloud services and SaaS applications.

id2.title: Conduct a risk assessment
id2.description: Systematically assess cybersecurity risks by likelihood and impact.
id2.firstStep: Perform a risk assessment for your 10 most critical systems.

pr1.title: Adopt a zero-trust approach
pr1.description: Implement the principle of "never trust, always verify" for all access.
pr1.firstStep: Start with MFA for all external access points and cloud services.

pr2.title: Establish an awareness program
pr2.description: Launch a continuous security awareness program with regular training sessions.
pr2.firstStep: Schedule an initial awareness training session for all employees.

de1.title: Implement monitoring
de1.description: Implement continuous monitoring of all critical systems and networks.
de1.firstStep: Start by monitoring your firewall logs and Active Directory events.

de2.title: Build a SIEM/SOC capability
de2.description: Implement a SIEM system or engage a managed SOC service.
de2.firstStep: Evaluate 2-3 managed SOC providers for your organization's profile.

rs1.title: Create an incident response plan
rs1.description: Develop a comprehensive IR plan with roles, processes, and communication templates.
rs1.firstStep: Define the IR team and create an escalation plan.

rs2.title: Conduct IR exercises
rs2.description: Perform regular tabletop exercises and technical IR drills.
rs2.firstStep: Schedule a ransomware tabletop exercise with management.

rc1.title: Create recovery plans
rc1.description: Document recovery plans for all critical systems.
rc1.firstStep: Create a recovery plan for your email system as a pilot.

rc2.title: Plan recovery tests
rc2.description: Test the recovery of critical systems at least quarterly.
rc2.firstStep: Schedule a full backup recovery test for next month.

au1.title: Implement modern password policy
au1.description: Adopt NIST-compliant password policies: minimum 12 characters, breach check, no forced rotation.
au1.firstStep: Review your current password policy against NIST SP 800-63B.

au2.title: Enable MFA across the board
au2.description: Enable TOTP or WebAuthn/FIDO2 for all user accounts.
au2.firstStep: Start with admin accounts and developer access.

sm1.title: Harden session security
sm1.description: Implement secure session configuration: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, appropriate timeouts.
sm1.firstStep: Review your cookie flags and enable HttpOnly and Secure.

ac1.title: Implement RBAC
ac1.description: Introduce role-based access control following the principle of least privilege.
ac1.firstStep: Document all roles and their required permissions.

ac2.title: Ensure server-side enforcement
ac2.description: Ensure all access controls are enforced server-side.
ac2.firstStep: Review 5 critical endpoints for missing server-side controls.

iv1.title: Adopt an input validation framework
iv1.description: Implement a centralized input validation library for all user inputs.
iv1.firstStep: Identify all input points and implement whitelist validation.

iv2.title: Enforce prepared statements
iv2.description: Replace all dynamic SQL queries with parameterized statements.
iv2.firstStep: Search for string concatenation in SQL queries and replace them.

cr1.title: Implement encryption strategy
cr1.description: Encrypt all sensitive data at rest and in transit using current algorithms.
cr1.firstStep: Inventory all locations where sensitive data is stored.

cr2.title: Modernize password hashing
cr2.description: Migrate to bcrypt/Argon2 with appropriate cost factors.
cr2.firstStep: Check which hashing algorithm your application currently uses.

el1.title: Implement secure error handling
el1.description: Display generic error messages and log details only server-side.
el1.firstStep: Search for stack traces in production responses and remove them.

el2.title: Establish security logging
el2.description: Log all security-relevant events (logins, errors, access denials).
el2.firstStep: Implement logging for failed login attempts and authorization errors.

el3.title: Implement API security
el3.description: Secure APIs with authentication, rate limiting, and input validation.
el3.firstStep: Implement rate limiting on all public API endpoints.
